leads.title: The Buddha becomes a Christian saint
leads.summary: The life of the Buddha passed through Manichaean and Arabic versions (Bilawhar wa-Būdhāsf) into the Georgian Balavariani and the Greek Barlaam and Ioasaph. Josaphat became a saint in the Christian calendar.

evidence.text: The name chain bodhisattva → Būdhāsaf → Yūdāsaf → Iōasaph is the lexical spine of the lead.

passages.text: וְאֶת בִּנְיָמִין֙ אֲחִ֣י יוֹסֵ֔ף לֹא שָׁלַ֥ח יַעֲקֹ֖ב אֶת אֶחָ֑יו כִּ֣י אָמַ֔ר פֶּן יִקְרָאֶ֖נּוּ אָסֽוֹן
וַיֹּ֕אמֶר לֹֽא יֵרֵ֥ד בְּנִ֖י עִמָּכֶ֑ם כִּֽי אָחִ֨יו מֵ֜ת וְה֧וּא לְבַדּ֣וֹ נִשְׁאָ֗ר וּקְרָאָ֤הוּ אָסוֹן֙ בַּדֶּ֨רֶךְ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר תֵּֽלְכוּ בָ֔הּ וְהוֹרַדְתֶּ֧ם אֶת שֵׂיבָתִ֛י בְּיָג֖וֹן שְׁאֽוֹלָה
וּלְקַחְתֶּ֧ם גַּם אֶת זֶ֛ה מֵעִ֥ם פָּנַ֖י וְקָרָ֣הוּ אָס֑וֹן וְהֽוֹרַדְתֶּ֧ם אֶת שֵׂיבָתִ֛י בְּרָעָ֖ה שְׁאֹֽלָה
וְכִֽי יִנָּצ֣וּ אֲנָשִׁ֗ים וְנָ֨גְפ֜וּ אִשָּׁ֤ה הָרָה֙ וְיָצְא֣וּ יְלָדֶ֔יהָ וְלֹ֥א יִהְיֶ֖ה אָס֑וֹן עָנ֣וֹשׁ יֵעָנֵ֗שׁ כַּֽאֲשֶׁ֨ר יָשִׁ֤ית עָלָיו֙ בַּ֣עַל הָֽאִשָּׁ֔ה וְנָתַ֖ן בִּפְלִלִֽים
וְאִם אָס֖וֹן יִהְיֶ֑ה וְנָתַתָּ֥ה נֶ֖פֶשׁ תַּ֥חַת נָֽפֶשׁ

passages.text: וַתֹּ֧אמֶר הַבְּכִירָ֛ה אֶל הַצְּעִירָ֖ה אָבִ֣ינוּ זָקֵ֑ן וְאִ֨ישׁ אֵ֤ין בָּאָ֨רֶץ֙ לָב֣וֹא עָלֵ֔ינוּ כְּדֶ֖רֶךְ כָּל הָאָֽרֶץ
וַתַּשְׁקֶ֧יןָ אֶת אֲבִיהֶ֛ן יַ֖יִן בַּלַּ֣יְלָה ה֑וּא וַתָּבֹ֤א הַבְּכִירָה֙ וַתִּשְׁכַּ֣ב אֶת אָבִ֔יהָ וְלֹֽא יָדַ֥ע בְּשִׁכְבָ֖הּ וּבְקׄוּמָֽהּ
וַֽיְהִי֙ מִֽמָּחֳרָ֔ת וַתֹּ֤אמֶר הַבְּכִירָה֙ אֶל הַצְּעִירָ֔ה הֵן שָׁכַ֥בְתִּי אֶ֖מֶשׁ אֶת אָבִ֑י נַשְׁקֶ֨נּוּ יַ֜יִן גַּם הַלַּ֗יְלָה וּבֹ֨אִי֙ שִׁכְבִ֣י עִמּ֔וֹ וּנְחַיֶּ֥ה מֵאָבִ֖ינוּ זָֽרַע
וַתֵּ֤לֶד הַבְּכִירָה֙ בֵּ֔ן וַתִּקְרָ֥א שְׁמ֖וֹ מוֹאָ֑ב ה֥וּא אֲבִֽי מוֹאָ֖ב עַד הַיּֽוֹם
וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָבָ֔ן לֹא יֵעָשֶׂ֥ה כֵ֖ן בִּמְקוֹמֵ֑נוּ לָתֵ֥ת הַצְּעִירָ֖ה לִפְנֵ֥י הַבְּכִירָֽה
וַיִּֽהְיוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י שָׁא֔וּל יוֹנָתָ֥ן וְיִשְׁוִ֖י וּמַלְכִּי שׁ֑וּעַ וְשֵׁם֙ שְׁתֵּ֣י בְנֹתָ֔יו שֵׁ֤ם הַבְּכִירָה֙ מֵרַ֔ב וְשֵׁ֥ם הַקְּטַנָּ֖ה מִיכַֽל

passages.text: כִּ֣י הַמַּגִּיד֩ לִ֨י לֵאמֹ֜ר הִנֵּה מֵ֣ת שָׁא֗וּל וְהֽוּא הָיָ֤ה כִמְבַשֵּׂר֙ בְּעֵינָ֔יו וָאֹחֲזָ֣ה ב֔וֹ וָאֶהְרְגֵ֖הוּ בְּצִֽקְלָ֑ג אֲשֶׁ֥ר לְתִתִּי ל֖וֹ בְּשֹׂרָֽה
וַיֹּ֧אמֶר ל֣וֹ יוֹאָ֗ב לֹא֩ אִ֨ישׁ בְּשֹׂרָ֤ה אַתָּה֙ הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֔ה וּבִשַּׂרְתָּ֖ בְּי֣וֹם אַחֵ֑ר וְהַיּ֤וֹם הַזֶּה֙ לֹ֣א תְבַשֵּׂ֔ר כִּֽי על עַל כֵּ֥ן בֶּן הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ מֵֽת

וַיֹּ֨סֶף ע֜וֹד אֲחִימַ֤עַץ בֶּן צָדוֹק֙ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֶל יוֹאָ֔ב וִ֣יהִי מָ֔ה אָרֻֽצָה נָּ֥א גַם אָ֖נִי אַחֲרֵ֣י הַכּוּשִׁ֑י וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יוֹאָ֗ב לָֽמָּה זֶּ֞ה אַתָּ֥ה רָץ֙ בְּנִ֔י וּלְכָ֖ה אֵין בְּשׂוֹרָ֥ה מֹצֵֽאת
וַיִּקְרָ֤א הַצֹּפֶה֙ וַיַּגֵּ֣ד לַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אִם לְבַדּ֖וֹ בְּשׂוֹרָ֣ה בְּפִ֑יו וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ הָל֖וֹךְ וְקָרֵֽב
וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ הַצֹּפֶ֔ה אֲנִ֤י רֹאֶה֙ אֶת מְרוּצַ֣ת הָרִאשׁ֔וֹן כִּמְרֻצַ֖ת אֲחִימַ֣עַץ בֶּן צָד֑וֹק וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אִֽישׁ ט֣וֹב זֶ֔ה וְאֶל בְּשׂוֹרָ֥ה טוֹבָ֖ה יָבֽוֹא

וַיֹּאמְרוּ֩ אִ֨ישׁ אֶל רֵעֵ֜הוּ לֹֽא כֵ֣ן אֲנַ֣חְנוּ עֹשִׂ֗ים הַיּ֤וֹם הַזֶּה֙ יוֹם בְּשֹׂרָ֣ה ה֔וּא וַאֲנַ֣חְנוּ מַחְשִׁ֗ים וְחִכִּ֛ינוּ עַד א֥וֹר הַבֹּ֖קֶר וּמְצָאָ֣נוּ עָו֑וֹן וְעַתָּה֙ לְכ֣וּ וְנָבֹ֔אָה וְנַגִּ֖ידָה בֵּ֥ית הַמֶּֽלֶךְ

leads.title: dâth: a word shared by Esther and Moses
leads.summary: דָּת (dâth, H1881) occurs in 21 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Esther (19) and Moses (1). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: וַיֹּאמַ֗ר יְהוָ֞ה מִסִּינַ֥י בָּא֙ וְזָרַ֤ח מִשֵּׂעִיר֙ לָ֔מוֹ הוֹפִ֨יעַ֙ מֵהַ֣ר פָּארָ֔ן וְאָתָ֖ה מֵרִבְבֹ֣ת קֹ֑דֶשׁ מִֽימִינ֕וֹ אשדת אֵ֥שׁ דָּ֖ת לָֽמוֹ
וַֽיִּתְּנ֣וּ אֶת דָּתֵ֣י הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ לַאֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנֵי֙ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וּפַחֲו֖וֹת עֵ֣בֶר הַנָּהָ֑ר וְנִשְּׂא֥וּ אֶת הָעָ֖ם וְאֶת בֵּֽית הָאֱלֹהִֽים
וְהַשְּׁתִיָּ֥ה כַדָּ֖ת אֵ֣ין אֹנֵ֑ס כִּי כֵ֣ן יִסַּ֣ד הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ עַ֚ל כָּל רַ֣ב בֵּית֔וֹ לַעֲשׂ֖וֹת כִּרְצ֥וֹן אִישׁ וָאִֽישׁ
וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לַחֲכָמִ֖ים יֹדְעֵ֣י הָֽעִתִּ֑ים כִּי כֵן֙ דְּבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לִפְנֵ֕י כָּל יֹדְעֵ֖י דָּ֥ת וָדִֽין
כְּדָת֙ מַֽה לַּעֲשׂ֔וֹת בַּמַּלְכָּ֖ה וַשְׁתִּ֑י עַ֣ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא עָשְׂתָ֗ה אֶֽת מַאֲמַר֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ בְּיַ֖ד הַסָּרִיסִֽים

אִם עַל הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ ט֗וֹב יֵצֵ֤א דְבַר מַלְכוּת֙ מִלְּפָנָ֔יו וְיִכָּתֵ֛ב בְּדָתֵ֥י פָֽרַס וּמָדַ֖י וְלֹ֣א יַעֲב֑וֹר אֲשֶׁ֨ר לֹֽא תָב֜וֹא וַשְׁתִּ֗י לִפְנֵי֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ וּמַלְכוּתָהּ֙ יִתֵּ֣ן הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לִרְעוּתָ֖הּ הַטּוֹבָ֥ה מִמֶּֽנָּה

וַיְהִ֗י בְּהִשָּׁמַ֤ע דְּבַר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ וְדָת֔וֹ וּֽבְהִקָּבֵ֞ץ נְעָר֥וֹת רַבּ֛וֹת אֶל שׁוּשַׁ֥ן הַבִּירָ֖ה אֶל יַ֣ד הֵגָ֑י וַתִּלָּקַ֤ח אֶסְתֵּר֙ אֶל בֵּ֣ית הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אֶל יַ֥ד הֵגַ֖י שֹׁמֵ֥ר הַנָּשִֽׁים

וּבְהַגִּ֡יעַ תֹּר֩ נַעֲרָ֨ה וְנַעֲרָ֜ה לָב֣וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֗וֹשׁ מִקֵּץ֩ הֱי֨וֹת לָ֜הּ כְּדָ֤ת הַנָּשִׁים֙ שְׁנֵ֣ים עָשָׂ֣ר חֹ֔דֶשׁ כִּ֛י כֵּ֥ן יִמְלְא֖וּ יְמֵ֣י מְרוּקֵיהֶ֑ן שִׁשָּׁ֤ה חֳדָשִׁים֙ בְּשֶׁ֣מֶן הַמֹּ֔ר וְשִׁשָּׁ֤ה חֳדָשִׁים֙ בַּבְּשָׂמִ֔ים וּבְתַמְרוּקֵ֖י הַנָּשִֽׁים

וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הָמָן֙ לַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ יֶשְׁנ֣וֹ עַם אֶחָ֗ד מְפֻזָּ֤ר וּמְפֹרָד֙ בֵּ֣ין הָֽעַמִּ֔ים בְּכֹ֖ל מְדִינ֣וֹת מַלְכוּתֶ֑ךָ וְדָתֵיהֶ֞ם שֹׁנ֣וֹת מִכָּל עָ֗ם וְאֶת דָּתֵ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֵינָ֣ם עֹשִׂ֔ים וְלַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֵין שֹׁוֶ֖ה לְהַנִּיחָֽם
פַּתְשֶׁ֣גֶן הַכְּתָ֗ב לְהִנָּ֤תֵֽן דָּת֙ בְּכָל מְדִינָ֣ה וּמְדִינָ֔ה גָּל֖וּי לְכָל הָֽעַמִּ֑ים לִהְי֥וֹת עֲתִדִ֖ים לַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה
הָֽרָצִ֞ים יָצְא֤וּ דְחוּפִים֙ בִּדְבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וְהַדָּ֥ת נִתְּנָ֖ה בְּשׁוּשַׁ֣ן הַבִּירָ֑ה וְהַמֶּ֤לֶךְ וְהָמָן֙ יָשְׁב֣וּ לִשְׁתּ֔וֹת וְהָעִ֥יר שׁוּשָׁ֖ן נָבֽוֹכָה
וּבְכָל מְדִינָ֣ה וּמְדִינָ֗ה מְקוֹם֙ אֲשֶׁ֨ר דְּבַר הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ וְדָתוֹ֙ מַגִּ֔יעַ אֵ֤בֶל גָּדוֹל֙ לַיְּהוּדִ֔ים וְצ֥וֹם וּבְכִ֖י וּמִסְפֵּ֑ד שַׂ֣ק וָאֵ֔פֶר יֻצַּ֖ע לָֽרַבִּֽים

וְאֶת פַּתְשֶׁ֣גֶן כְּתָֽב הַ֠דָּת אֲשֶׁר נִתַּ֨ן בְּשׁוּשָׁ֤ן לְהַשְׁמִידָם֙ נָ֣תַן ל֔וֹ לְהַרְא֥וֹת אֶת אֶסְתֵּ֖ר וּלְהַגִּ֣יד לָ֑הּ וּלְצַוּ֣וֹת עָלֶ֗יהָ לָב֨וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֧לֶךְ לְהִֽתְחַנֶּן ל֛וֹ וּלְבַקֵּ֥שׁ מִלְּפָנָ֖יו עַל עַמָּֽהּ

כָּל עַבְדֵ֣י הַמֶּ֡לֶךְ וְעַם מְדִינ֨וֹת הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ יֽוֹדְעִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֣ר כָּל אִ֣ישׁ וְאִשָּׁ֡ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר יָבֽוֹא אֶל הַמֶּלֶךְ֩ אֶל הֶחָצֵ֨ר הַפְּנִימִ֜ית אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא יִקָּרֵ֗א אַחַ֤ת דָּתוֹ֙ לְהָמִ֔ית לְ֠בַד מֵאֲשֶׁ֨ר יֽוֹשִׁיט ל֥וֹ הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ אֶת שַׁרְבִ֥יט הַזָּהָ֖ב וְחָיָ֑ה וַאֲנִ֗י לֹ֤א נִקְרֵ֨אתי֙ לָב֣וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ זֶ֖ה שְׁלוֹשִׁ֥ים יֽוֹם

לֵךְ֩ כְּנ֨וֹס אֶת כָּל הַיְּהוּדִ֜ים הַֽנִּמְצְאִ֣ים בְּשׁוּשָׁ֗ן וְצ֣וּמוּ עָ֠לַי וְאַל תֹּאכְל֨וּ וְאַל תִּשְׁתּ֜וּ שְׁלֹ֤שֶׁת יָמִים֙ לַ֣יְלָה וָי֔וֹם גַּם אֲנִ֥י וְנַעֲרֹתַ֖י אָצ֣וּם כֵּ֑ן וּבְכֵ֞ן אָב֤וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא כַדָּ֔ת וְכַאֲשֶׁ֥ר אָבַ֖דְתִּי אָבָֽדְתִּי

passages.text: וּמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א שֹׁמַ֛עַת אֶת שֵׁ֥מַע שְׁלֹמֹ֖ה לְשֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֑ה וַתָּבֹ֥א לְנַסֹּת֖וֹ בְּחִידֽוֹת
וַתֵּ֨רֶא֙ מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֔א אֵ֖ת כָּל חָכְמַ֣ת שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה וְהַבַּ֖יִת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנָֽה

וַתִּתֵּ֨ן לַמֶּ֜לֶךְ מֵאָ֥ה וְעֶשְׂרִ֣ים כִּכַּ֣ר זָהָ֗ב וּבְשָׂמִ֛ים הַרְבֵּ֥ה מְאֹ֖ד וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה לֹא בָא֩ כַבֹּ֨שֶׂם הַה֥וּא עוֹד֙ לָרֹ֔ב אֲשֶׁר נָתְנָ֥ה מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֖א לַמֶּ֥לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹֽה
וְהַמֶּ֨לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֜ה נָתַ֣ן לְמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א אֶת כָּל חֶפְצָהּ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שָׁאָ֔לָה מִלְּבַד֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נָֽתַן לָ֔הּ כְּיַ֖ד הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה וַתֵּ֛פֶן וַתֵּ֥לֶךְ לְאַרְצָ֖הּ הִ֥יא וַעֲבָדֶֽיהָ

וּמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א שָֽׁמְעָה֮ אֶת שֵׁ֣מַע שְׁלֹמֹה֒ וַתָּב֣וֹא לְנַסּוֹת֩ אֶת שְׁלֹמֹ֨ה בְחִיד֜וֹת בִּירֽוּשָׁלִַ֗ם בְּחַ֣יִל כָּבֵ֣ד מְאֹ֡ד וּ֠גְמַלִּים נֹשְׂאִ֨ים בְּשָׂמִ֧ים וְזָהָ֛ב לָרֹ֖ב וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה וַתָּבוֹא֙ אֶל שְׁלֹמֹ֔ה וַתְּדַבֵּ֣ר עִמּ֔וֹ אֵ֛ת כָּל אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָיָ֖ה עִם לְבָבָֽהּ
וַתֵּ֨רֶא֙ מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֔א אֵ֖ת חָכְמַ֣ת שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה וְהַבַּ֖יִת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנָֽה
וַתִּתֵּ֨ן לַמֶּ֜לֶךְ מֵאָ֥ה וְעֶשְׂרִ֣ים כִּכַּ֣ר זָהָ֗ב וּבְשָׂמִ֛ים לָרֹ֥ב מְאֹ֖ד וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה וְלֹ֤א הָיָה֙ כַּבֹּ֣שֶׂם הַה֔וּא אֲשֶׁר נָתְנָ֥ה מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֖א לַמֶּ֥לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹֽה
וְהַמֶּ֨לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֜ה נָתַ֣ן לְמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א אֶת כָּל חֶפְצָהּ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שָׁאָ֔לָה מִלְּבַ֖ד אֲשֶׁר הֵבִ֣יאָה אֶל הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וַֽתַּהֲפֹ֛ךְ וַתֵּ֥לֶךְ לְאַרְצָ֖הּ הִ֥יא וַעֲבָדֶֽיהָ
גַּ֚ם וַשְׁתִּ֣י הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה עָשְׂתָ֖ה מִשְׁתֵּ֣ה נָשִׁ֑ים בֵּ֚ית הַמַּלְכ֔וּת אֲשֶׁ֖ר לַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֽוֹשׁ
לְ֠הָבִיא אֶת וַשְׁתִּ֧י הַמַּלְכָּ֛ה לִפְנֵ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ בְּכֶ֣תֶר מַלְכ֑וּת לְהַרְא֨וֹת הָֽעַמִּ֤ים וְהַשָּׂרִים֙ אֶת יָפְיָ֔הּ כִּֽי טוֹבַ֥ת מַרְאֶ֖ה הִֽיא
וַתְּמָאֵ֞ן הַמַּלְכָּ֣ה וַשְׁתִּ֗י לָבוֹא֙ בִּדְבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אֲשֶׁ֖ר בְּיַ֣ד הַסָּרִיסִ֑ים וַיִּקְצֹ֤ף הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ מְאֹ֔ד וַחֲמָת֖וֹ בָּעֲרָ֥ה בֽוֹ
כְּדָת֙ מַֽה לַּעֲשׂ֔וֹת בַּמַּלְכָּ֖ה וַשְׁתִּ֑י עַ֣ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא עָשְׂתָ֗ה אֶֽת מַאֲמַר֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ בְּיַ֖ד הַסָּרִיסִֽים

וַיֹּ֣אמֶר מומכן מְמוּכָ֗ן לִפְנֵ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ וְהַשָּׂרִ֔ים לֹ֤א עַל הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ לְבַדּ֔וֹ עָוְתָ֖ה וַשְׁתִּ֣י הַמַּלְכָּ֑ה כִּ֤י עַל כָּל הַשָּׂרִים֙ וְעַל כָּל הָ֣עַמִּ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֕ר בְּכָל מְדִינ֖וֹת הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֽוֹשׁ
כִּֽי יֵצֵ֤א דְבַר הַמַּלְכָּה֙ עַל כָּל הַנָּשִׁ֔ים לְהַבְז֥וֹת בַּעְלֵיהֶ֖ן בְּעֵינֵיהֶ֑ן בְּאָמְרָ֗ם הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֡וֹשׁ אָמַ֞ר לְהָבִ֨יא אֶת וַשְׁתִּ֧י הַמַּלְכָּ֛ה לְפָנָ֖יו וְלֹא בָֽאָה
וְֽהַיּ֨וֹם הַזֶּ֜ה תֹּאמַ֣רְנָה שָׂר֣וֹת פָּֽרַס וּמָדַ֗י אֲשֶׁ֤ר שָֽׁמְעוּ֙ אֶת דְּבַ֣ר הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה לְכֹ֖ל שָׂרֵ֣י הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וּכְדַ֖י בִּזָּי֥וֹן וָקָֽצֶף

passages.text: ר֥וּחַ יְהוָ֖ה דִּבֶּר בִּ֑י וּמִלָּת֖וֹ עַל לְשׁוֹנִֽי
הֲנִסָּ֬ה דָבָ֣ר אֵלֶ֣יךָ תִּלְאֶ֑ה וַעְצֹ֥ר בְּ֝מִלִּ֗ין מִ֣י יוּכָֽל
כּ֭וֹשֵׁל יְקִימ֣וּן מִלֶּ֑יךָ וּבִרְכַּ֖יִם כֹּרְע֣וֹת תְּאַמֵּֽץ
הַלְהוֹכַ֣ח מִלִּ֣ים תַּחְשֹׁ֑בוּ וּ֝לְר֗וּחַ אִמְרֵ֥י נֹאָֽשׁ
הֲלֹא הֵ֣ם י֭וֹרוּךָ יֹ֣אמְרוּ לָ֑ךְ וּ֝מִלִּבָּ֗ם יוֹצִ֥אוּ מִלִּֽים
הֲלֹא אֹ֭זֶן מִלִּ֣ין תִּבְחָ֑ן וְ֝חֵ֗ךְ אֹ֣כֶל יִטְעַם לֽוֹ
שִׁמְע֣וּ שָׁ֭מוֹעַ מִלָּתִ֑י וְ֝אַֽחֲוָתִ֗י בְּאָזְנֵיכֶֽם
הוֹכֵ֣חַ בְּ֭דָבָר לֹ֣א יִסְכּ֑וֹן וּ֝מִלִּ֗ים לֹא יוֹעִ֥יל בָּֽם
כִּֽי תָשִׁ֣יב אֶל אֵ֣ל רוּחֶ֑ךָ וְהֹצֵ֖אתָ מִפִּ֣יךָ מִלִּֽין
גַּ֤ם אָנֹכִי֮ כָּכֶ֪ם אֲדַ֫בֵּ֥רָה ל֤וּ יֵ֪שׁ נַפְשְׁכֶ֡ם תַּ֤חַת נַפְשִׁ֗י אַחְבִּ֣ירָה עֲלֵיכֶ֣ם בְּמִלִּ֑ים וְאָנִ֥יעָה עֲ֝לֵיכֶ֗ם בְּמ֣וֹ רֹאשִֽׁי
עַד אָ֤נָה תְּשִׂימ֣וּן קִנְצֵ֣י לְמִלִּ֑ין תָּ֝בִ֗ינוּ וְאַחַ֥ר נְדַבֵּֽר
עַד אָ֭נָה תּוֹגְי֣וּן נַפְשִׁ֑י וּֽתְדַכְּאוּנַ֥נִי בְמִלִּֽים
מִֽי יִתֵּ֣ן אֵ֭פוֹ וְיִכָּתְב֣וּן מִלָּ֑י מִֽי יִתֵּ֖ן בַּסֵּ֣פֶר וְיֻחָֽקוּ
שִׁמְע֣וּ שָׁ֭מוֹעַ מִלָּתִ֑י וּתְהִי זֹ֝֗את תַּנְח֥וּמֹֽתֵיכֶֽם
אֵ֭דְעָה מִלִּ֣ים יַעֲנֵ֑נִי וְ֝אָבִ֗ינָה מַה יֹּ֥אמַר לִֽי

passages.text: וְיִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל אָהַ֤ב אֶת יוֹסֵף֙ מִכָּל בָּנָ֔יו כִּֽי בֶן זְקֻנִ֥ים ה֖וּא ל֑וֹ וְעָ֥שָׂה ל֖וֹ כְּתֹ֥נֶת פַּסִּֽים
וַֽיְהִ֕י כַּֽאֲשֶׁר בָּ֥א יוֹסֵ֖ף אֶל אֶחָ֑יו וַיַּפְשִׁ֤יטוּ אֶת יוֹסֵף֙ אֶת כֻּתָּנְתּ֔וֹ אֶת כְּתֹ֥נֶת הַפַּסִּ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָלָֽיו
וַֽיְשַׁלְּח֞וּ אֶת כְּתֹ֣נֶת הַפַּסִּ֗ים וַיָּבִ֨יאוּ֙ אֶל אֲבִיהֶ֔ם וַיֹּאמְר֖וּ זֹ֣את מָצָ֑אנוּ הַכֶּר נָ֗א הַכְּתֹ֧נֶת בִּנְךָ֛ הִ֖וא אִם לֹֽא

passages.text: עֲשֵׂ֤ה לְךָ֙ תֵּבַ֣ת עֲצֵי גֹ֔פֶר קִנִּ֖ים תַּֽעֲשֶׂ֣ה אֶת הַתֵּבָ֑ה וְכָֽפַרְתָּ֥ אֹתָ֛הּ מִבַּ֥יִת וּמִח֖וּץ בַּכֹּֽפֶר
וְזֶ֕ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר תַּֽעֲשֶׂ֖ה אֹתָ֑הּ שְׁלֹ֧שׁ מֵא֣וֹת אַמָּ֗ה אֹ֚רֶךְ הַתֵּבָ֔ה חֲמִשִּׁ֤ים אַמָּה֙ רָחְבָּ֔הּ וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים אַמָּ֖ה קוֹמָתָֽהּ
צֹ֣הַר תַּֽעֲשֶׂ֣ה לַתֵּבָ֗ה וְאֶל אַמָּה֙ תְּכַלֶ֣נָּה מִלְמַ֔עְלָה וּפֶ֥תַח הַתֵּבָ֖ה בְּצִדָּ֣הּ תָּשִׂ֑ים תַּחְתִּיִּ֛ם שְׁנִיִּ֥ם וּשְׁלִשִׁ֖ים תַּֽעֲשֶֽׂהָ
וַהֲקִמֹתִ֥י אֶת בְּרִיתִ֖י אִתָּ֑ךְ וּבָאתָ֙ אֶל הַתֵּבָ֔ה אַתָּ֕ה וּבָנֶ֛יךָ וְאִשְׁתְּךָ֥ וּנְשֵֽׁי בָנֶ֖יךָ אִתָּֽךְ
וּמִכָּל הָ֠חַי מִֽכָּל בָּשָׂ֞ר שְׁנַ֧יִם מִכֹּ֛ל תָּבִ֥יא אֶל הַתֵּבָ֖ה לְהַחֲיֹ֣ת אִתָּ֑ךְ זָכָ֥ר וּנְקֵבָ֖ה יִֽהְיֽוּ
וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ לְנֹ֔חַ בֹּֽא אַתָּ֥ה וְכָל בֵּיתְךָ֖ אֶל הַתֵּבָ֑ה כִּֽי אֹתְךָ֥ רָאִ֛יתִי צַדִּ֥יק לְפָנַ֖י בַּדּ֥וֹר הַזֶּֽה
וַיָּ֣בֹא נֹ֗חַ וּ֠בָנָיו וְאִשְׁתּ֧וֹ וּנְשֵֽׁי בָנָ֛יו אִתּ֖וֹ אֶל הַתֵּבָ֑ה מִפְּנֵ֖י מֵ֥י הַמַּבּֽוּל
שְׁנַ֨יִם שְׁנַ֜יִם בָּ֧אוּ אֶל נֹ֛חַ אֶל הַתֵּבָ֖ה זָכָ֣ר וּנְקֵבָ֑ה כַּֽאֲשֶׁ֛ר צִוָּ֥ה אֱלֹהִ֖ים אֶת נֹֽחַ
בְּעֶ֨צֶם הַיּ֤וֹם הַזֶּה֙ בָּ֣א נֹ֔חַ וְשֵׁם וְחָ֥ם וָיֶ֖פֶת בְּנֵי נֹ֑חַ וְאֵ֣שֶׁת נֹ֗חַ וּשְׁלֹ֧שֶׁת נְשֵֽׁי בָנָ֛יו אִתָּ֖ם אֶל הַתֵּבָֽה
וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ אֶל נֹ֖חַ אֶל הַתֵּבָ֑ה שְׁנַ֤יִם שְׁנַ֨יִם֙ מִכָּל הַבָּשָׂ֔ר אֲשֶׁר בּ֖וֹ ר֥וּחַ חַיִּֽים
וַֽיְהִ֧י הַמַּבּ֛וּל אַרְבָּעִ֥ים י֖וֹם עַל הָאָ֑רֶץ וַיִּרְבּ֣וּ הַמַּ֗יִם וַיִּשְׂאוּ֙ אֶת הַתֵּבָ֔ה וַתָּ֖רָם מֵעַ֥ל הָאָֽרֶץ
וַיִּגְבְּר֥וּ הַמַּ֛יִם וַיִּרְבּ֥וּ מְאֹ֖ד עַל הָאָ֑רֶץ וַתֵּ֥לֶךְ הַתֵּבָ֖ה עַל פְּנֵ֥י הַמָּֽיִם

וַיִּ֜מַח אֶֽת כָּל הַיְק֣וּם אֲשֶׁ֣ר עַל פְּנֵ֣י הָֽאֲדָמָ֗ה מֵאָדָ֤ם עַד בְּהֵמָה֙ עַד רֶ֨מֶשׂ֙ וְעַד ע֣וֹף הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וַיִּמָּח֖וּ מִן הָאָ֑רֶץ וַיִשָּׁ֧אֶר אַךְ נֹ֛חַ וַֽאֲשֶׁ֥ר אִתּ֖וֹ בַּתֵּבָֽה
וַיִּזְכֹּ֤ר אֱלֹהִים֙ אֶת נֹ֔חַ וְאֵ֤ת כָּל הַֽחַיָּה֙ וְאֶת כָּל הַבְּהֵמָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר אִתּ֖וֹ בַּתֵּבָ֑ה וַיַּעֲבֵ֨ר אֱלֹהִ֥ים ר֨וּחַ֙ עַל הָאָ֔רֶץ וַיָּשֹׁ֖כּוּ הַמָּֽיִם
וַתָּ֤נַח הַתֵּבָה֙ בַּחֹ֣דֶשׁ הַשְּׁבִיעִ֔י בְּשִׁבְעָה עָשָׂ֥ר י֖וֹם לַחֹ֑דֶשׁ עַ֖ל הָרֵ֥י אֲרָרָֽט

וְשַׂמְתָּ֥ אוֹתָ֛ם שְׁתַּ֥יִם מַֽעֲרָכ֖וֹת שֵׁ֣שׁ הַֽמַּעֲרָ֑כֶת עַ֛ל הַשֻּׁלְחָ֥ן הַטָּהֹ֖ר לִפְנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה
וּבָנִ֨יתָ מִזְבֵּ֜חַ לַיהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֗יךָ עַ֣ל רֹ֧אשׁ הַמָּע֛וֹז הַזֶּ֖ה בַּמַּֽעֲרָכָ֑ה וְלָֽקַחְתָּ֙ אֶת הַפָּ֣ר הַשֵּׁנִ֔י וְהַעֲלִ֣יתָ עוֹלָ֔ה בַּעֲצֵ֥י הָאֲשֵׁרָ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר תִּכְרֹֽת
וַיַּעַרְכ֨וּ פְלִשְׁתִּ֜ים לִקְרַ֣את יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל וַתִּטֹּשׁ֙ הַמִּלְחָמָ֔ה וַיִּנָּ֥גֶף יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לִפְנֵ֣י פְלִשְׁתִּ֑ים וַיַּכּ֤וּ בַמַּֽעֲרָכָה֙ בַּשָּׂדֶ֔ה כְּאַרְבַּ֥עַת אֲלָפִ֖ים אִֽישׁ
וַיָּ֤רָץ אִישׁ בִּנְיָמִן֙ מֵהַמַּ֣עֲרָכָ֔ה וַיָּבֹ֥א שִׁלֹ֖ה בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֑וּא וּמַדָּ֣יו קְרֻעִ֔ים וַאֲדָמָ֖ה עַל רֹאשֽׁוֹ
וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הָאִ֜ישׁ אֶל עֵלִ֗י אָֽנֹכִי֙ הַבָּ֣א מִן הַמַּעֲרָכָ֔ה וַאֲנִ֕י מִן הַמַּעֲרָכָ֖ה נַ֣סְתִּי הַיּ֑וֹם וַיֹּ֛אמֶר מֶֽה הָיָ֥ה הַדָּבָ֖ר בְּנִֽי

וַֽיַּעֲמֹ֗ד וַיִּקְרָא֙ אֶל מַעַרְכֹ֣ת יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָהֶ֔ם לָ֥מָּה תֵצְא֖וּ לַעֲרֹ֣ךְ מִלְחָמָ֑ה הֲל֧וֹא אָנֹכִ֣י הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֗י וְאַתֶּם֙ עֲבָדִ֣ים לְשָׁא֔וּל בְּרוּ לָכֶ֥ם אִ֖ישׁ וְיֵרֵ֥ד אֵלָֽי
וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֔י אֲנִ֗י חֵרַ֛פְתִּי אֶת מַעַרְכ֥וֹת יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֑ה תְּנוּ לִ֣י אִ֔ישׁ וְנִֽלָּחֲמָ֖ה יָֽחַד

וַיַּשְׁכֵּ֨ם דָּוִ֜ד בַּבֹּ֗קֶר וַיִּטֹּ֤שׁ אֶת הַצֹּאן֙ עַל שֹׁמֵ֔ר וַיִּשָּׂ֣א וַיֵּ֔לֶךְ כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר צִוָּ֖הוּ יִשָׁ֑י וַיָּבֹא֙ הַמַּעְגָּ֔לָה וְהַחַ֗יִל הַיֹּצֵא֙ אֶל הַמַּ֣עֲרָכָ֔ה וְהֵרֵ֖עוּ בַּמִּלְחָמָֽה
וַתַּעֲרֹ֤ךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ וּפְלִשְׁתִּ֔ים מַעֲרָכָ֖ה לִקְרַ֥את מַעֲרָכָֽה
וַיִּטֹּשׁ֩ דָּוִ֨ד אֶת הַכֵּלִ֜ים מֵעָלָ֗יו עַל יַד֙ שׁוֹמֵ֣ר הַכֵּלִ֔ים וַיָּ֖רָץ הַמַּעֲרָכָ֑ה וַיָּבֹ֕א וַיִּשְׁאַ֥ל לְאֶחָ֖יו לְשָׁלֽוֹם
וְה֣וּא מְדַבֵּ֣ר עִמָּ֗ם וְהִנֵּ֣ה אִ֣ישׁ הַבֵּנַ֡יִם עוֹלֶ֞ה גָּלְיָת֩ הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֨י שְׁמ֤וֹ מִגַּת֙ ממערות מִמַּעַרְכ֣וֹת פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים וַיְדַבֵּ֖ר כַּדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה וַיִּשְׁמַ֖ע דָּוִֽד

וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֗ד אֶֽל הָאֲנָשִׁ֞ים הָעֹמְדִ֣ים עִמּוֹ֮ לֵאמֹר֒ מַה יֵּעָשֶׂ֗ה לָאִישׁ֙ אֲשֶׁ֤ר יַכֶּה֙ אֶת הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֣י הַלָּ֔ז וְהֵסִ֥יר חֶרְפָּ֖ה מֵעַ֣ל יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל כִּ֣י מִ֗י הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֤י הֶֽעָרֵל֙ הַזֶּ֔ה כִּ֣י חֵרֵ֔ף מַעַרְכ֖וֹת אֱלֹהִ֥ים חַיִּֽים
גַּ֧ם אֶֽת הָאֲרִ֛י גַּם הַדּ֖וֹב הִכָּ֣ה עַבְדֶּ֑ךָ וְֽ֠הָיָה הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֨י הֶעָרֵ֤ל הַזֶּה֙ כְּאַחַ֣ד מֵהֶ֔ם כִּ֣י חֵרֵ֔ף מַעַרְכֹ֖ת אֱלֹהִ֥ים חַיִּֽים
וַיֹּ֤אמֶר דָּוִד֙ אֶל הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֔י אַתָּה֙ בָּ֣א אֵלַ֔י בְּחֶ֖רֶב וּבַחֲנִ֣ית וּבְכִיד֑וֹן וְאָנֹכִ֣י בָֽא אֵלֶ֗יךָ בְּשֵׁם֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת אֱלֹהֵ֛י מַעַרְכ֥וֹת יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר חֵרַֽפְתָּ

leads.title: The Kalam cosmological argument
leads.summary: The argument that the universe began and so has a cause, developed by the mutakallimūn and al-Ghazali, was revived and named by William Lane Craig in analytic philosophy of religion.

passages.ref: W. L. Craig, The Kalām Cosmological Argument (1979)

leads.title: Panchatantra to Kalila wa-Dimna
leads.summary: The Sanskrit Panchatantra was translated into Middle Persian (Burzoy, 6th c.), then Arabic (Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, 8th c.), then into Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and most European languages.

leads.title: Kumarbi cycle and Hesiod's Theogony
leads.summary: Both have the same succession myth: Anu, Kumarbi, Teshub in the Hurro-Hittite cycle and Ouranos, Kronos, Zeus in Hesiod, including a sky god castrated by his successor.

leads.title: Atrahasis: the flood (Middle Babylonian fragments, the boat and the birds) ↔ The Flood (full read)
leads.summary: 7 shared motifs, found by the separate reads; not yet compared side by side.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Birds released to find dry land (weight 6.6); Exact dimensions of the vessel are specified (weight 6.5); Animals taken aboard in pairs (weight 6.5); Vessel has several decks, a side door and a roof opening or window (weight 6.2); Vessel sealed with pitch or bitumen (weight 6.2); Hero privately warned of the coming flood by a deity (weight 5.8); Hero's family saved with him (weight 5.4). Pair score 43.4.

Only in Atrahasis: the flood (Middle Babylonian fragments, the boat and the birds): The flood hero is told: 'Destroy your house, build a boat; spurn property, save life'; Once the hero has entered the boat its door is sealed shut; A dove released from the boat flies off and returns because she has exhausted her wings and found no place; From his throne the high god takes an oath to annihilate (humankind) totally; While those boarding eat and drink, the flood hero alone is heavy-hearted, knowing what is coming; The flood boat is to be built on a circular plan, its length equal to its breadth, like a giant coracle; A god appears to a man in a dream and gives him practical instructions, which he carries out; Warning spoken to a wall or reed hut so the hero overhears.

Only in The Flood (full read): Clean animals taken aboard by sevens, unclean by pairs; Flood events given exact calendar dates (year of hero's life, month, day); Rain or flood lasts forty days and forty nights; A dove returns with an olive leaf in its beak; Seven days pass between the warning or boarding and the onset of the flood; Angels object that the new human will corrupt the earth and shed blood while they praise God; When the water overflowed God carried 'you' in the running ship (al-jariya) as a reminder for retaining ears [divergence between the texts]; What sets the flood in motion: God's decision on violence, or the rejected prophet's prayer [divergence between the texts]; How the ark is described [divergence between the texts]; What the flood hero does when the vessel comes to rest [divergence between the texts]; What God says of later generations after the flood: no repeat, or punishment to come [contrast between the texts]; How the flood waters are stopped and subside [divergence between the texts]; and 39 more.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: God regrets having made humankind and is grieved in his heart (weight 7.3); A raven is sent out and does not return (goes to and fro) (weight 7.3); God sends a wind (ruah) over the earth to make the waters subside (weight 7.3); God himself shuts the vessel's door behind the hero (weight 7.3); What the flood hero does when the vessel comes to rest (weight 7.1); Whether the flood hero speaks to his people before the flood (weight 6.8); Deity resolves or promises not to repeat the destruction (weight 6.6); Birds released to find dry land (weight 6.6); Deity or gods smell the offering (weight 6.5); Exact dimensions of the vessel are specified (weight 6.5); Vessel comes to rest on a named mountain (weight 6.4); Waters pour both from the sky and from springs of the earth (weight 6.2); Vessel has several decks, a side door and a roof opening or window (weight 6.2); Vessel sealed with pitch or bitumen (weight 6.2); Hero offers sacrifice after leaving the vessel (weight 6.2); Hero builds a vessel on divine instruction (weight 6.2); Deity decides to destroy humankind (weight 6.1); All others perish (weight 5.9); Hero privately warned of the coming flood by a deity (weight 5.8); Hero's family saved with him (weight 5.4). Pair score 130.3.

Only in Utnapishtim's flood (Gilgamesh, Standard Babylonian Tablet XI:8-206): The divine warning commands: abandon riches, spurn property and save life; After the flood all humankind has returned to clay; the plain is flat as a roof; Instead of the flood, a lion, a wolf, famine or plague should have diminished the people; The mother goddess bars the god who caused the flood from the offering, for he acted without counsel; Huge measured quantities of bitumen, pitch and oil are poured into the kiln and the hull; The hero slaughters oxen and sheep and gives the workers beer, oil and wine like river water, so they feast as at the New Year festival; What sets the flood in motion: God's decision on violence, or the rejected prophet's prayer; The chief god sees the boat and is enraged that a living being escaped: 'no man should survive!'; What the ark contains; Besides kin and animals, craftsmen of every skill are taken aboard; The god gives the hero a cover story: Enlil hates me, I am going down to the Apsû, and he will rain abundance on you (bread-cakes in the morning, a torrent of wheat in the evening) - an ambiguous promise of the coming flood; How the ark is described; and 61 more.

Only in The Flood (full read): Clean animals taken aboard by sevens, unclean by pairs; Flood events given exact calendar dates (year of hero's life, month, day); Rain or flood lasts forty days and forty nights; A dove returns with an olive leaf in its beak; Seven days pass between the warning or boarding and the onset of the flood; Angels object that the new human will corrupt the earth and shed blood while they praise God; When the water overflowed God carried 'you' in the running ship (al-jariya) as a reminder for retaining ears [divergence between the texts]; What sets the flood in motion: God's decision on violence, or the rejected prophet's prayer [divergence between the texts]; How the ark is described [divergence between the texts]; What the flood hero does when the vessel comes to rest [divergence between the texts]; What God says of later generations after the flood: no repeat, or punishment to come [contrast between the texts]; How the flood waters are stopped and subside [divergence between the texts]; and 26 more.

Only in Utnapishtim's flood (Gilgamesh, Standard Babylonian Tablet XI:8-206): The divine warning commands: abandon riches, spurn property and save life; After the flood all humankind has returned to clay; the plain is flat as a roof; Instead of the flood, a lion, a wolf, famine or plague should have diminished the people; The mother goddess bars the god who caused the flood from the offering, for he acted without counsel; Huge measured quantities of bitumen, pitch and oil are poured into the kiln and the hull; The hero slaughters oxen and sheep and gives the workers beer, oil and wine like river water, so they feast as at the New Year festival; What sets the flood in motion: God's decision on violence, or the rejected prophet's prayer; The chief god sees the boat and is enraged that a living being escaped: 'no man should survive!'; What the ark contains; Besides kin and animals, craftsmen of every skill are taken aboard; The god gives the hero a cover story: Enlil hates me, I am going down to the Apsû, and he will rain abundance on you (bread-cakes in the morning, a torrent of wheat in the evening) - an ambiguous promise of the coming flood; How the ark is described; and 77 more.

Only in Blessing of Noah, blood laws and the covenant of the bow: God requires the life of a human even from an animal that kills; God makes a covenant with humans and all living creatures; Eating animals permitted to humans after the flood; Whoever sheds human blood, by man shall his blood be shed, because humans bear God's image [divergence between the texts]; The same religion (din) was enjoined on Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus and the Prophet: establish it and do not divide; The sign left after the flood: the rainbow, or the ark [divergence between the texts]; Whoever sheds human blood, by man shall his blood be shed, because humans bear God's image; The sign the flood leaves for later generations [divergence between the texts]; Humans given rule over animals; Eating blood is forbidden; Humanity made in the image or likeness of the deity; Divine blessing: be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth.

Only in Sayings on strife, bribes, friends and the silent fool: Better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in his folly; A bribe is a stone of charm (even hen) in the eyes of its owner; wherever he turns he prospers; A joyful heart is good medicine, but a broken spirit dries up the bones; The crucible is for silver and the furnace for gold, but YHWH tests hearts; Whoever returns evil for good, evil will not depart from his house; Wisdom is before the face of the discerning, but the eyes of a fool are on the ends of the earth; Grandchildren are the crown of the aged and fathers the glory of their sons; Why is there a price in the hand of a fool to buy wisdom when he has no heart?; A rebuke goes deeper into a discerning man than a hundred blows into a fool; Even a fool who keeps silent is counted wise; The beginning of strife is like letting out water; quit before the quarrel breaks out; A wise slave will rule over a shameful son and share the inheritance among the brothers; and 10 more.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: The proud one plans to ascend to heaven, raise his throne above the stars of El and make himself like Elyon (weight 6.5); The monster sets up a throne, is named king and judges lawsuits, challenging the god's kingship (weight 6.2). Pair score 12.7.

Only in Anzu covets supremacy and steals the tablet of destinies while Enlil bathes (Anzû SB I b+56-b+87): A rebel against the high god vows, in a string of first-person 'I will' clauses, to take and to command [divergence between the texts]; The rebel seizes the token of supreme power while the high god is bathing, undressed, with his crown laid on the throne; A rebel resolves in his heart, in a string of first-person 'I will' boasts, to seize the throne and command all the gods; The hero, unsatisfied with honours, secretly sets his sights on ruling the whole world; In the divine assembly the high god asks which of the gods will go and slay the monster, promising him the greatest name; When the token of rule is stolen, deathly silence falls and the sanctuary is stripped of its divine radiance; A tablet of destinies whose possession confers the divine powers and rule.

Only in Ea has seen the dead; the gods bellow; battle with the cut-off Ullikummi and his boast (CTH 345.I.3.1 §25-34): A god is distressed at having seen the dead in the dark earth, standing like dust; All the gods assemble and bellow at the monster like cattle; The monster declares he will go up to kingship in heaven, take the city and the holy temples and pour the gods out of heaven; The god Ea is king of wisdom, creator of discernment, sage of the gods; The stone child is set like a spear on the right shoulder of the giant who bears the world (Upelluri), and grows there; The storm god's bulls Šeri(šu) and Tella are fetched, horns anointed, tail gilded, for his battle wagon; The chief god refuses help and the wise god (Enki) grants it.

Only in BD 125 (pNu): the second declaration of innocence, addressed to the 42 judges: Denial: the speaker did no wrong although he saw evil; Denial: the speaker has not diminished (encroached on) fields or interfered with the field survey; Denial with exception: the speaker has not quarrelled, except over his own property; Denial / prohibition of eavesdropping or spying on others; A list of renounced sins in fixed form: not stealing, not killing, not lying / slandering, not committing adultery; Denial: the speaker has not driven off the cattle of the god's estate nor blocked a god in his procession; The divine judges of the dead live on the evildoers and drink their blood on the day of reckoning; Denial: the speaker has not shortened the grain measure or the land measure nor tampered with the weights or plummet of the balance; The dead person recites before the divine judges a long series of denials, 'I have not done X', to prove his innocence.

Only in BD 125 (pMaiherperi): the 42 addresses: Denial: the speaker has not made anyone go hungry, made anyone weep, or caused anyone pain; A series of 'I/they shall not' clauses covering theft, adultery, killing and lying, spoken before an authority [divergence between the texts].

(weight 7.1); The just one's front, back and middle are pure; no limb of his is without Maat (weight 7.1); A demon of the underworld (Babi, the Devouress) lives on the entrails of the great or devours the condemned on the day of reckoning (weight 6.8); The dead declares himself without wrong, without sin and without any witness against him; there is no one he has harmed (weight 6.8); In the judgment of the dead the heart is weighed on a balance against Maat; Anubis checks the plummet and Thoth records the result (weight 6.8); The dead person comes to the Hall of the Two Truths (Maat) to be judged before the great god and separated from the sins he has committed (weight 6.6); The dead person claims to know the names of the god and his judges, and this knowledge protects him from their harm (weight 6.6); Who shall ascend the mountain of YHWH? He who has clean hands and a pure heart and has not sworn deceitfully (weight 6.2). Pair score 68.5.

Only in BD 125 (pNu): address to the gods of the hall, works of mercy, purity and the examination at the gate: A balance set upright / just balances set up for the judgment; Giving food to the hungry (water, clothing, a ferry) as the deed that justifies before the judge; Self-praise: I did what people speak of and what the gods are pleased with; I satisfied the god with what he loves; A fixed day on which the characters or deeds of the dead are reckoned up before the god of the dead; The judge's messengers inflict slaughter and punishment, and there is no mercy in their faces; The dead has purified himself in a sacred lake (the southern pool, the field of locusts) where the gods' crew washes; Catalogue of the righteous man: no eating on the mountains, no idols, no adultery, no menstrual intercourse, no oppression, returns pledges, feeds the hungry, clothes the naked, no interest; Who witnesses against the dead at the judgment (no witness against me / their own limbs and skins) [divergence between the texts]; Denial: the speaker has not reviled a god, the king or the god of his town.

Only in BD 125 (pYuya): address to the gods, examination, gate names, Thoth, rubric: At the judgment the dead state whether they fed the hungry [divergence between the texts]; The dwelling or throne of the highest god rests on (primeval) water; Each part of the gate (jambs, lintel, bolt, doorkeeper, floor, even the soles of the feet) refuses passage until the dead says its secret name; Rubric formula: 'truly effective, (proven) millions of times'; The dwelling of Osiris has a roof of fire, walls of living uraeus serpents and a floor of flood water; The ritual image is drawn in ochre on clean ground on which no pig, goat (or lion, horse) has trodden; Whoever has this book made for him prospers with his children, is a confidant of the king and is turned back at no gate of the West; Thoth, the 'interpreter of the Two Lands', receives the purified dead and announces him to Osiris; The justified dead is told: your bread is the Udjat eye, your beer is the Udjat eye, your offering on earth is the Udjat eye; Rubric: the spell is to be recited clean and pure, dressed in fresh linen, shod in white sandals, eyes painted and anointed with myrrh, after offering; God tests the hearts and the kidneys (inner self).

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: The judge's messengers inflict slaughter and punishment, and there is no mercy in their faces (weight 7.3); The dead has purified himself in a sacred lake (the southern pool, the field of locusts) where the gods' crew washes (weight 7.3); Self-praise of the just: I gave bread to the hungry, water to the thirsty, clothes to the naked (and a ferry to the boatless) (weight 7.3); The just one lives on Maat and feeds on Maat; the divine judges too are said to live on Maat, with no lie in their bodies (weight 7.1); Gate-guardians interrogate the dead: who are you, what is your name, where did you pass, what did you see, what did they give you? (weight 7.1); The just one's front, back and middle are pure; no limb of his is without Maat (weight 7.1); A demon of the underworld (Babi, the Devouress) lives on the entrails of the great or devours the condemned on the day of reckoning (weight 6.8); The dead declares himself without wrong, without sin and without any witness against him; there is no one he has harmed (weight 6.8); In the judgment of the dead the heart is weighed on a balance against Maat; Anubis checks the plummet and Thoth records the result (weight 6.8); Who shall ascend the mountain of YHWH? He who has clean hands and a pure heart and has not sworn deceitfully (weight 6.2). Pair score 69.9.

Only in BD 125 (pNu): address to the gods of the hall, works of mercy, purity and the examination at the gate: A balance set upright / just balances set up for the judgment; Giving food to the hungry (water, clothing, a ferry) as the deed that justifies before the judge; Self-praise: I did what people speak of and what the gods are pleased with; I satisfied the god with what he loves; A fixed day on which the characters or deeds of the dead are reckoned up before the god of the dead; Catalogue of the righteous man: no eating on the mountains, no idols, no adultery, no menstrual intercourse, no oppression, returns pledges, feeds the hungry, clothes the naked, no interest; Who witnesses against the dead at the judgment (no witness against me / their own limbs and skins) [divergence between the texts]; Denial: the speaker has not reviled a god, the king or the god of his town; The dead person comes to the Hall of the Two Truths (Maat) to be judged before the great god and separated from the sins he has committed; The dead person claims to know the names of the god and his judges, and this knowledge protects him from their harm.

Only in BD 125 (pTurin 1791): address to the gods, works of mercy, gate and Thoth, late version: At the judgment the dead state whether they fed the hungry [divergence between the texts]; Each part of the gate (jambs, lintel, bolt, doorkeeper, floor, even the soles of the feet) refuses passage until the dead says its secret name; The dwelling of Osiris has a roof of fire, walls of living uraeus serpents and a floor of flood water; Thoth, the 'interpreter of the Two Lands', receives the purified dead and announces him to Osiris; The justified dead is told: your bread is the Udjat eye, your beer is the Udjat eye, your offering on earth is the Udjat eye; God tests the hearts and the kidneys (inner self).

(weight 7.1); The just one's front, back and middle are pure; no limb of his is without Maat (weight 7.1); Each part of the gate (jambs, lintel, bolt, doorkeeper, floor, even the soles of the feet) refuses passage until the dead says its secret name (weight 7.1); The dwelling of Osiris has a roof of fire, walls of living uraeus serpents and a floor of flood water (weight 6.8); A demon of the underworld (Babi, the Devouress) lives on the entrails of the great or devours the condemned on the day of reckoning (weight 6.8); Thoth, the 'interpreter of the Two Lands', receives the purified dead and announces him to Osiris (weight 6.8); The dead declares himself without wrong, without sin and without any witness against him; there is no one he has harmed (weight 6.8); The justified dead is told: your bread is the Udjat eye, your beer is the Udjat eye, your offering on earth is the Udjat eye (weight 6.8); In the judgment of the dead the heart is weighed on a balance against Maat; Anubis checks the plummet and Thoth records the result (weight 6.8); Who shall ascend the mountain of YHWH? evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Oath of innocence: 'If I have done this... let the enemy pursue and trample me' (weight 7.7). Pair score 7.7.

Only in Niḫriya remembered; 'die for the king; death shall be your limit' (CTH 123 §§10-20): In the king's time of need the sworn man must 'bite the dark earth and hold it' (stand his ground to the death); Loyalty formula: when things go hard for the king, the sworn man must die for him; 'death shall be your limit'; The gods are to keep watch on the deed of treason; The excuse that one was forced or powerless is put forward for going over to the other side; The excuse that one was forced or powerless is put forward for going over to the other side [contrast between the texts]; Reproaching followers who hang back, the leader recalls how he escaped a crisis without them; The sworn may not excuse joining rebels or traitors by saying 'they brought me by force' or 'they compelled me'; The king reproaches the sworn man: when things were hard he was not with him; did the king not escape alone from Niḫriya, stay behind alone at Alatarma?; The sworn must take the oath with their whole heart, not with the lips only, and teach it to their sons who come after; The overlord points the vassal to neighbouring kings who abandoned the treaty: 'later you will see what the great king does to them'; The vassal and his brothers are ready to die with (for) the king their lord; The vassal must not set another king or another lord over himself.

Only in Psalm 7 - Shiggayon concerning Cush the Benjaminite: The congregation of peoples surrounds God as he takes his seat on high to judge; God whets his sword and strings his bow, preparing deadly fiery arrows; The wicked conceives mischief, is pregnant with trouble and gives birth to falsehood; They plot a plot, and God plots a plot; give the deniers respite a little; The evil plot encompasses only its own authors; God Most High (El Elyon), creator/possessor of heaven and earth; The enemy is like a lion that tears the speaker's soul or lurks in ambush; Call to God to arise (qumah YHWH) and save or judge; He who digs a pit or hides a net is caught in it himself; God tests the hearts and the kidneys (inner self); Superscription sets the psalm in a specific episode of David's life; Superscription contains an obscure musical or liturgical term (neginot, nehilot, sheminit, gittit, alamot, shiggayon, maskil, miktam, shoshannim...); and 1 more.

Only in The king did not reward me; an engraved word; guardians of the king's life; the king's direst hour (CTH 123 §§21-28): Picture of the king's direst hour: no groom left to harness his horses, the charioteer leaping from the chariot, the chamberlain fleeing, not even a gate-dog left nor an arrow to shoot; The sworn may not say 'the king has not rewarded me; I will withdraw from these oaths'; In the decisive crisis the leader's own men run off and leave him; A follower's loyalty depends on being rewarded; unrewarded, he turns away; The oath is declared to be an engraved word ('this word shall be an engraved limma for you'); The sworn man with his wife, children and subjects must be watchmen and guardians of the king's life, never guardians or onlookers of evil; The king reproaches the sworn man: when things were hard he was not with him; did the king not escape alone from Niḫriya, stay behind alone at Alatarma?; Curse formula: 'the oath gods shall hunt (pursue) you' (NĪŠ DINGIR.MEŠ parḫeškandu); The vassal and his brothers are ready to die with (for) the king their lord.

Only in Telipinu Proclamation W2: the assembly, the law of succession and the law protecting the royal family: The council must tell a king plotting against his kin to read the precedent on the tablet: bloodshed in the past and its divine punishment; The king and his council are forbidden to kill members of the royal family ('do not say I will purge; you will only entangle yourself'); No burdened soul bears another's burden; even a relative will not carry any of it [divergence between the texts]; The house, fields, vineyards, servants and herds of an executed prince may not be taken; taking them is not right; Succession law: a first-rank son becomes king; failing him a second-rank son; failing any son, the husband taken for the first-rank daughter; The servants of the princes grow corrupt, devour their masters' houses, plot against them and shed their blood; The assembly of the realm (Hittite panku, tuliya) is convened to judge crimes within the royal family and to restrain the king; Named conspirators are held up to the officials as a warning sign ('let them be a sign before you'); While the king's sons, brothers, in-laws, kinsmen and troops stood united, the small land grew and the enemy was held subdued; Those who incite rebellion must be seized, put in fetters and delivered to the king, or killed; Each person dies for his own sin.

Only in Census of the second generation on the plains of Moab: A second census counts the new generation by clans; The family of Amram / Imran and Miriam / Maryam [divergence between the texts]; Land divided by lot and in proportion to tribal size; Mother of Moses, Aaron and Miriam named (Jochebed, born to Levi in Egypt); Miriam / Maryam named as the daughter of Amram / ʿImran; Priests die for offering 'strange fire'; Daughters petition and win the right to inherit when there is no son; Whole adult generation condemned to die in the desert; only children enter; A lone daughter is named in a male genealogy (Dinah, Serah); The earth opens its mouth and swallows rebels alive into Sheol.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: A man refuses the sexual advances of a powerful woman and suffers her revenge (weight 6.8); The master's wife tries to seduce the hero (weight 6.1). Pair score 13.0.

Only in Ašertu tries to seduce the storm god; he tells Elkunirša (CTH 342.1.1): A god takes from a victim the hair of his head, the sight of his eyes and the hearing of his ears; A grieving goddess installs mourners and laments for seven years; The elder god tells the young god to go and humiliate his own wife; The storm god taunts a goddess: 'I killed your 77 children, I killed 88'; The young god goes to the elder god's tent and reports that the elder god's wife tried to seduce him; A god becomes heavy and drowsy (sleepy); How the husband answers when told of his wife's advances to the young man [divergence between the texts]; The goddess whose advances were refused threatens the young god: 'be behind me ... I will press you down with my words, pierce you with my spindle'.

Only in Tale of Two Brothers (Papyrus d'Orbiney 1,1-6,3): the household, the seduction and the false accusation: The woman makes herself look beaten (with fat and bandages), lies feigning sickness, does not pour water on her husband's hands or light the lamp, to support her accusation; In her false accusation the woman quotes her own proposal word for word as the hero's, and her own (fictive) refusal citing kinship; The false accuser tells her husband she will kill herself if he lets the accused live; The cattle speak to their herdsman and tell him where the pasture is good, and he understands them; Under the hero's care the master's cattle thrive exceedingly and multiply their calves; The hero runs away from his own brother, who pursues him to kill him; Refusing, the hero tells the woman she is like a mother to him and her husband like a father, and calls her proposal a great crime; The hero promises to tell no one of the woman's proposal and orders her never to speak of it again; The deceived husband (elder brother) sharpens his spear and waits behind the stable door to kill the hero on his return; The temptress promises the young man fine clothes as reward for lying with her; As each cow enters the stable it speaks to its herdsman, warning him that a man stands behind the door to kill him: 'flee!'; A tale opens with two brothers 'of one mother and one father', the elder a householder, the younger his helper; and 9 more.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: The god has made the sufferer an ill-placed man at the king's gate, his case unsuccessful before men (weight 7.7); The worshipper asks which of his god's favours he has not known since childhood (weight 7.7); The sufferer asks that his offences be made known to him by dream, by a seeress or by liver omen, so that he can recognise them (weight 7.7); At night in his bed no pleasant dream comes to the sufferer and his name does not appear for good (weight 7.3); The king has lain at the god's feet since he was small (weight 7.3); The sufferer asks whether his god wrote his illness down for him from his mother's womb (weight 7.3); Address to the personal god: 'You are my father who begot me; lift up my face' (weight 7.1); What befalls creatures is written beforehand on a heavenly tablet or in a book (weight 7.1); The deity alone can become angry and then relent, have pity and forgive (weight 6.5); The sufferer asks his god to show him his sins so that he may confess them openly at the city gate (weight 6.4). Pair score 72.2.

Only in The man's plea to his personal god, illness and unknown sin (CTH 372 §9-19): He who switches weights and cheats with the scales or measures is punished; the honest weigher is rewarded; Saying: a man's god is a man's shepherd who does not desert him and gives him food and water; The sufferer says he drifts like a boat on the river and does not know his destination; The king tells a goddess: 'I have no mother, you are my mother; I have no father, you are my father'; In adversity the god takes the sufferer's hand, slaps him awake with the right hand and raises his head with the left.

Only in Kantuzzili's prayer to the Sun god (CTH 373): Life is bound up with death and death with life; a child of mortality does not live forever; The sufferer protests that he never swore falsely or broke an oath, never ate what is holy to his god, never parted an ox or sheep from its pen, and never ate his bread or drank his water alone; The angry god has turned his eyes aside to another place and no longer lets the man act; Through illness the sufferer's house has become a house of fear and his soul drifts elsewhere; The merchant who falsifies the scales before the sun god is contrasted with the sufferer who has done nothing to his god; A trader cheats with the scales or the measure; The righteous did not eat his morsel alone without sharing with the orphan; Only the gods dwell forever with the sun; man's days are numbered; The petitioner asks the sun god, who reaches heaven and earth, to go to the angry god wherever he is and deliver the man's words; The sufferer asks what he has done to his god and goddess: he is treated like one who does not fear his god; The dead person recites before the divine judges a long series of denials, 'I have not done X', to prove his innocence.

Only in Muršili II's hymn and prayer to the Sun goddess of Arinna in plague and war (CTH 376.1): The deity is invoked for seven days in each of her cities; The deity is told not to let her own name be humbled by the land's defeat; The absent deity is called back to her temple, whether she is in heaven, in the sea or roaming the mountains, with cedar, oil, bread and libations; The assembled people answer the king's prayer with 'Let it be so!'; A destroying calamity does not single out the wrongdoers but strikes all [divergence between the texts]; The hostile neighbours do not honour the gods, transgress the oath sworn by the gods and seek to rob the temples; If the offerers die, the gods will later hold it against the king as a sin and ask 'Why do you not give us bread and libations?'; The king asks the deity for life, health, vigour, long years, sons, daughters, grandchildren, obedience, and the growth of grain, vines, cattle, sheep, horses and men; The land is said to dangle from the tip of a needle; Former vassal lands cast off the patron goddess, refuse their tribute and make war on the land; A Hittite king destroys Aleppo and Babylon and carries their deportees and goods to Hattusa; No other god is weighty and great compared to the deity; her name is weightiest among names and her divinity among the gods; and 10 more.

Only in Rebellion after the spies' report and the forty-year sentence: Those who slandered the land die by plague; People have tested God 'ten times'; Forty years of wandering, a year for each day of scouting [divergence between the texts]; God threatens to destroy a people and put another in its place [divergence between the texts]; Two faithful spies dissent from the majority [divergence between the texts]; People ordered to fight complain to God and wish to be spared the battle; People attack without God's ark or leader and are routed; After the people's rebellion the prophet intercedes for them or asks to be separated from them [divergence between the texts]; People propose appointing a leader to go back to Egypt; Caleb has 'another spirit' and follows God fully; God offers to destroy the people and make a nation of the hero instead; The townsfolk say 'we augur ill of you' and threaten to stone the messengers; they reply 'your omen is with you'; and 10 more.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: The afflicting deity is told: take this one (the carrier animal) for yourself, and we give you another (a goat, a pure mouse) to eat (weight 7.3); Formula: take the evil out of him and give it to the evil men, the enemies; to the patients give life, vigour and long years (weight 7.1); Analogy of the launderers: as they clean the linen and pluck off the lint until it is white, so may the gods clean the evil illness out of this man's body (weight 7.1); White wool or a bowstring is drawn over the patient from the feet up to the head and down the back, then taken off and laid in a basket, pulling the evil out of every limb (weight 7.1); Tin wrapped in a bowstring is tied on the patient's right hand and foot, then wound on a mouse, which is released to carry the evil over high mountains, deep valleys and far roads (weight 7.1); Wood and grain are roasted and the fire quenched with water: as I have quenched this, so may the evil be quenched over the patients (weight 7.1); The afflicting deity is told to stop fighting the patients and fight this bolt (a model door-bolt) instead, and drive the evil away with it (weight 7.1); Living goat bears the people's sins away into the wilderness (weight 6.2). Pair score 55.9.

Only in Ambazzi's ritual for Alauwaima, the mouse released, a goat in its place, metals for good speech before the gods (CTH 391.1 §13-28): The deity is asked to give the patient life, health, vigour, long years and the sight of the eyes; A little of every metal and stone (silver, gold, lapis, carnelian, iron, tin, copper, bronze) is strewn for the deity, who is asked to speak good for the patient before all the gods; Choice portions of the victim (right ear, liver, heart, right shoulder, breast, hoof) are roasted and set before the gods on bread and leaves; the rest is cooked and eaten by the participants.
Ambazzi's ritual for Zarniza and Tarpatassa, quenching, wool, the launderers, the mouse (CTH 391.1 §1-12): tagged by Claude (model), reading the Hittite.
Ambazzi's ritual for Alauwaima, the mouse released, a goat in its place, metals for good speech before the gods (CTH 391.1 §13-28): tagged by Claude (model), reading the Hittite.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: The afflicting deity is told: take this one (the carrier animal) for yourself, and we give you another (a goat, a pure mouse) to eat (weight 7.3); Formula: take the evil out of him and give it to the evil men, the enemies; to the patients give life, vigour and long years (weight 7.1); Analogy of the launderers: as they clean the linen and pluck off the lint until it is white, so may the gods clean the evil illness out of this man's body (weight 7.1); White wool or a bowstring is drawn over the patient from the feet up to the head and down the back, then taken off and laid in a basket, pulling the evil out of every limb (weight 7.1); Tin wrapped in a bowstring is tied on the patient's right hand and foot, then wound on a mouse, which is released to carry the evil over high mountains, deep valleys and far roads (weight 7.1); Wood and grain are roasted and the fire quenched with water: as I have quenched this, so may the evil be quenched over the patients (weight 7.1); The afflicting deity is told to stop fighting the patients and fight this bolt (a model door-bolt) instead, and drive the evil away with it (weight 7.1); Living goat bears the people's sins away into the wilderness (weight 6.2). Pair score 55.9.

Only in Ambazzi's ritual for Tarpatassa 'who stands in front', the second pure mouse (CTH 391.1 §29-43): A little of every metal and stone (silver, gold, lapis, carnelian, iron, tin, copper, bronze) is strewn for the deity, who is asked to speak good for the patient before all the gods; Choice portions of the victim (right ear, liver, heart, right shoulder, breast, hoof) are roasted and set before the gods on bread and leaves; the rest is cooked and eaten by the participants.
Ambazzi's ritual for Zarniza and Tarpatassa, quenching, wool, the launderers, the mouse (CTH 391.1 §1-12): tagged by Claude (model), reading the Hittite.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: The afflicting deity is told: take this one (the carrier animal) for yourself, and we give you another (a goat, a pure mouse) to eat (weight 7.3); A little of every metal and stone (silver, gold, lapis, carnelian, iron, tin, copper, bronze) is strewn for the deity, who is asked to speak good for the patient before all the gods (weight 7.3); Formula: take the evil out of him and give it to the evil men, the enemies; to the patients give life, vigour and long years (weight 7.1); Analogy of the launderers: as they clean the linen and pluck off the lint until it is white, so may the gods clean the evil illness out of this man's body (weight 7.1); White wool or a bowstring is drawn over the patient from the feet up to the head and down the back, then taken off and laid in a basket, pulling the evil out of every limb (weight 7.1); Tin wrapped in a bowstring is tied on the patient's right hand and foot, then wound on a mouse, which is released to carry the evil over high mountains, deep valleys and far roads (weight 7.1); Wood and grain are roasted and the fire quenched with water: as I have quenched this, so may the evil be quenched over the patients (weight 7.1); The afflicting deity is told to stop fighting the patients and fight this bolt (a model door-bolt) instead, and drive the evil away with it (weight 7.1); Choice portions of the victim (right ear, liver, heart, right shoulder, breast, hoof) are roasted and set before the gods on bread and leaves; the rest is cooked and eaten by the participants (weight 6.6); Living goat bears the people's sins away into the wilderness (weight 6.2). Pair score 69.9.

Only in Ambazzi's ritual for Alauwaima, the mouse released, a goat in its place, metals for good speech before the gods (CTH 391.1 §13-28): The deity is asked to give the patient life, health, vigour, long years and the sight of the eyes.

וְהַשֹּׂרֵ֣ף אֹתָ֔ם יְכַבֵּ֣ס בְּגָדָ֔יו וְרָחַ֥ץ אֶת בְּשָׂר֖וֹ בַּמָּ֑יִם וְאַחֲרֵי כֵ֖ן יָב֥וֹא אֶל הַֽמַּחֲנֶֽה

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: The man who led away the scapegoat or burned the remains washes before re-entering the camp (weight 7.7). Pair score 7.7.

Only in Ašḫella's ritual, days two to four, eat in a god's way; salt water and two fires; the colophon (CTH 394 §6-9): Animals are slaughtered in the open field: 'O god, eat and drink in a god's way, and leave nothing to man'; The god who made the plague is fed and asked to be at peace with the land and army of Ḫatti and turn to them in kindness; Leaving the rite, the participants wash their hands in water with salt, light two fires and walk between them; A ewe that a ram has not yet gone to is offered (to the Sun god); While the god is being served, no one sets the god's vessels on the ground or picks them up again: it is not right; Metal spoils purified by passing through fire, others through water; Whether the deity eats the offered flesh, or the offerers and the poor do [divergence between the texts]; The participants 'drink the god' three times standing, then drink the gods who are kindly to them; A text ends with a note on its source or on where it was written.

Only in The Day of Atonement and the goat for Azazel: A goat is designated by lot 'for Azazel', a named wilderness recipient; Priest confesses the people's sins over the head of a live animal; High priest may enter the inner sanctuary behind the veil only on the annual day of atonement; High priest wears plain linen garments to enter the holy of holies; Cloud of incense covers the ark cover so the priest does not die; Lots cast over two goats to decide their roles; No one may be in the tent while the high priest makes atonement in the sanctuary; Blood rites purge the sanctuary and altar of the people's impurities and transgressions; Annual Day of Atonement on the tenth of the seventh month, with self-affliction and total rest; God appears in a cloud above the ark cover (kapporet); What the annual fast is tied to [divergence between the texts]; Blood or water sprinkled seven times; and 2 more.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: A pot waved over the patients is called the substitute for their heads and broken; they smash another vessel with their feet, breaking all the evil words and curses (weight 7.7); The patients' bodies are wiped with a 'plant of the Sun' named tiwariya, wiping off the evil words of mouth and tongue (weight 7.3); Seven standing stones (huwaši) are set between two fires and kicked over: as these stones fall, so may the words of mouth and tongue that came on the patients fall (weight 7.3); Water is poured into an ox horn and sealed by the patients: only when the ancient kings return and examine the land and its customs may the seal be broken (weight 7.3); The patients pour water with natron over their heads and wash their hands and eyes (weight 7.3); After passing through the fire the patients throw off their fine garments and the Old Woman takes them (weight 7.3); Fires are lit to right and left and the patients pass through the middle of the fire (weight 7.3); A text ends with a note on its source or on where it was written (weight 4.2). Pair score 56.0.

Only in Maštigga ritual, second manuscript group, salamander to the sealed horn and colophon of Ḫanikkuili (CTH 404.1.II §20-44): A clay vessel of Šaušga with oil, wool and barley is held under the patients' garment: may it release them to wellbeing and life and hide the evil away in an evil thing; A sheep is declared the patients' nakkušši (carrier of evil) with mouth and tongue, presented to the Sun, but not killed: the Old Woman takes it for herself; A salamander wrapped in blue and red wool is waved over the patients: may its swift foot carry off the evil tongue on its back and with its teeth; Seven copper (or bronze) nails are driven into the ground: may the evil be nailed down with its mouth and tongue, with the Sun's help; Seven vessels filled with wine, oil, honey, fruit, sinew, salt and fat are emptied one by one into the hearth and broken: may it break with mouth and tongue; The exalted Sun god is declared to stand behind (guarantee the treatment of) mouth and tongue; The substitute animal is slaughtered down into a dug pit, laid in it with sweet bread and wine, and covered with earth; An animal (sheep, black sheep, puppy) is held over the patients and declared their substitute (tarpalli-) for their heads and whole persons.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: A clay vessel of Šaušga with oil, wool and barley is held under the patients' garment: may it release them to wellbeing and life and hide the evil away in an evil thing (weight 7.3); Seven copper (or bronze) nails are driven into the ground: may the evil be nailed down with its mouth and tongue, with the Sun's help (weight 7.3); A sheep is declared the patients' nakkušši (carrier of evil) with mouth and tongue, presented to the Sun, but not killed: the Old Woman takes it for herself (weight 7.3); A salamander wrapped in blue and red wool is waved over the patients: may its swift foot carry off the evil tongue on its back and with its teeth (weight 7.3); Seven vessels filled with wine, oil, honey, fruit, sinew, salt and fat are emptied one by one into the hearth and broken: may it break with mouth and tongue (weight 7.3); The exalted Sun god is declared to stand behind (guarantee the treatment of) mouth and tongue (weight 7.3); The substitute animal is slaughtered down into a dug pit, laid in it with sweet bread and wine, and covered with earth (weight 7.1); An animal (sheep, black sheep, puppy) is held over the patients and declared their substitute (tarpalli-) for their heads and whole persons (weight 6.6). Pair score 57.7.

Only in Maštigga ritual, clay and cumin, the salamander and puppy, Šaušga's vessel, the carrier sheep and the seven nails (CTH 404.1.I §26-38): The patients place their hand on the bread, cheese and wine before the Old Woman breaks and offers it; Analogic spell: as this clay will not return to the riverbank, black cumin will not turn white nor become another seed, and this dough will not go into the gods' bread, so may the evil tongue not go into the patients' bodies; The patients spit into the mouth of the substitute animal: 'you have spat out the evil curses'; The Old Woman sprinkles the patients with water and waves dough over them: 'be pure again of mouth and tongue'; Living goat bears the people's sins away into the wilderness.

Only in Maštigga ritual, second manuscript group, salamander to the sealed horn and colophon of Ḫanikkuili (CTH 404.1.II §20-44): A pot waved over the patients is called the substitute for their heads and broken; they smash another vessel with their feet, breaking all the evil words and curses; Seven standing stones (huwaši) are set between two fires and kicked over: as these stones fall, so may the words of mouth and tongue that came on the patients fall; The patients' bodies are wiped with a 'plant of the Sun' named tiwariya, wiping off the evil words of mouth and tongue; After passing through the fire the patients throw off their fine garments and the Old Woman takes them; Fires are lit to right and left and the patients pass through the middle of the fire; The patients pour water with natron over their heads and wash their hands and eyes; Water is poured into an ox horn and sealed by the patients: only when the ancient kings return and examine the land and its customs may the seal be broken; A text ends with a note on its source or on where it was written.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: A clay vessel of Šaušga with oil, wool and barley is held under the patients' garment: may it release them to wellbeing and life and hide the evil away in an evil thing (weight 7.3); Seven copper (or bronze) nails are driven into the ground: may the evil be nailed down with its mouth and tongue, with the Sun's help (weight 7.3); Analogic spell: as this clay will not return to the riverbank, black cumin will not turn white nor become another seed, and this dough will not go into the gods' bread, so may the evil tongue not go into the patients' bodies (weight 7.3); A salamander wrapped in blue and red wool is waved over the patients: may its swift foot carry off the evil tongue on its back and with its teeth (weight 7.3); A sheep is declared the patients' nakkušši (carrier of evil) with mouth and tongue, presented to the Sun, but not killed: the Old Woman takes it for herself (weight 7.3); Seven vessels filled with wine, oil, honey, fruit, sinew, salt and fat are emptied one by one into the hearth and broken: may it break with mouth and tongue (weight 7.3); The exalted Sun god is declared to stand behind (guarantee the treatment of) mouth and tongue (weight 7.3); The Old Woman sprinkles the patients with water and waves dough over them: 'be pure again of mouth and tongue' (weight 7.1); The patients spit into the mouth of the substitute animal: 'you have spat out the evil curses' (weight 7.1); An animal (sheep, black sheep, puppy) is held over the patients and declared their substitute (tarpalli-) for their heads and whole persons (weight 6.6). Pair score 72.1.

Only in Maštigga ritual, clay and cumin, the salamander and puppy, Šaušga's vessel, the carrier sheep and the seven nails (CTH 404.1.I §26-38): The patients place their hand on the bread, cheese and wine before the Old Woman breaks and offers it; The substitute animal is slaughtered down into a dug pit, laid in it with sweet bread and wine, and covered with earth; Living goat bears the people's sins away into the wilderness.

Only in Maštigga ritual, third manuscript group for a single patient, the tongues nailed on Mount Amanakkipalu (CTH 404.1.III): Seven tongues of clay are fixed into the ground and the practitioner declares that father Sun has nailed down the tongues of the day of quarrel (on Mount Amanakkipalu); Seven standing stones (huwaši) are set between two fires and kicked over: as these stones fall, so may the words of mouth and tongue that came on the patients fall; The patients' bodies are wiped with a 'plant of the Sun' named tiwariya, wiping off the evil words of mouth and tongue; After passing through the fire the patients throw off their fine garments and the Old Woman takes them; Fires are lit to right and left and the patients pass through the middle of the fire; White and black wool wrapped in fat, called tiššatwa, is held over the patients to take away what they said with mouth and tongue; The patients pour water with natron over their heads and wash their hands and eyes; Water is poured into an ox horn and sealed by the patients: only when the ancient kings return and examine the land and its customs may the seal be broken; A text ends with a note on its source or on where it was written.
Maštigga ritual, clay and cumin, the salamander and puppy, Šaušga's vessel, the carrier sheep and the seven nails (CTH 404.1.I §26-38): tagged by Claude (model), reading the Hittite.
Maštigga ritual, third manuscript group for a single patient, the tongues nailed on Mount Amanakkipalu (CTH 404.1.III): tagged by Claude (model), reading the Hittite.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: A clay vessel of Šaušga with oil, wool and barley is held under the patients' garment: may it release them to wellbeing and life and hide the evil away in an evil thing (weight 7.3); Seven copper (or bronze) nails are driven into the ground: may the evil be nailed down with its mouth and tongue, with the Sun's help (weight 7.3); Seven standing stones (huwaši) are set between two fires and kicked over: as these stones fall, so may the words of mouth and tongue that came on the patients fall (weight 7.3); The patients' bodies are wiped with a 'plant of the Sun' named tiwariya, wiping off the evil words of mouth and tongue (weight 7.3); A sheep is declared the patients' nakkušši (carrier of evil) with mouth and tongue, presented to the Sun, but not killed: the Old Woman takes it for herself (weight 7.3); A salamander wrapped in blue and red wool is waved over the patients: may its swift foot carry off the evil tongue on its back and with its teeth (weight 7.3); Water is poured into an ox horn and sealed by the patients: only when the ancient kings return and examine the land and its customs may the seal be broken (weight 7.3); Seven vessels filled with wine, oil, honey, fruit, sinew, salt and fat are emptied one by one into the hearth and broken: may it break with mouth and tongue (weight 7.3); The patients pour water with natron over their heads and wash their hands and eyes (weight 7.3); After passing through the fire the patients throw off their fine garments and the Old Woman takes them (weight 7.3); The exalted Sun god is declared to stand behind (guarantee the treatment of) mouth and tongue (weight 7.3); Fires are lit to right and left and the patients pass through the middle of the fire (weight 7.3); An animal (sheep, black sheep, puppy) is held over the patients and declared their substitute (tarpalli-) for their heads and whole persons (weight 6.6); A text ends with a note on its source or on where it was written (weight 4.2). Pair score 99.0.

Only in Maštigga ritual, second manuscript group, salamander to the sealed horn and colophon of Ḫanikkuili (CTH 404.1.II §20-44): A pot waved over the patients is called the substitute for their heads and broken; they smash another vessel with their feet, breaking all the evil words and curses; The substitute animal is slaughtered down into a dug pit, laid in it with sweet bread and wine, and covered with earth.

Only in Maštigga ritual, third manuscript group for a single patient, the tongues nailed on Mount Amanakkipalu (CTH 404.1.III): Analogic spell: as this clay will not return to the riverbank, black cumin will not turn white nor become another seed, and this dough will not go into the gods' bread, so may the evil tongue not go into the patients' bodies; Seven tongues of clay are fixed into the ground and the practitioner declares that father Sun has nailed down the tongues of the day of quarrel (on Mount Amanakkipalu); White and black wool wrapped in fat, called tiššatwa, is held over the patients to take away what they said with mouth and tongue; The patients spit into the mouth of the substitute animal: 'you have spat out the evil curses'; The Old Woman sprinkles the patients with water and waves dough over them: 'be pure again of mouth and tongue'.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Mountains, rivers, springs, the great sea, heaven and earth, winds and clouds are named among the witnesses of a treaty or oath (weight 5.8); Heaven and earth called as witnesses against the people (weight 5.7). Pair score 11.5.

Only in Treaty of Tutḫaliya I with Šunaššura, Akkadian version KBo 28.110 (CTH 41.I.1): the ox and its stall, the tablet, the gods: The vassal is to trust a messenger only if his spoken words agree with the words written on the tablet he brings; A rival is condemned by his own earlier answer ('Just so!') to the very case now turned against him; The tablet of a vassal's former oath to a rival overlord is erased, the rival's word rejected and a new tablet made; The great king releases a land from a former overlord's oath, an act of 'release' (andurāru); When the vassal comes before the great king he may see the king's face and no grandee sits above him; Ox knows its owner and the ass its master's crib, but Israel does not know (animals wiser than God's people); Treaty curse: may the gods destroy the oath-breaker's name and seed from the earth; A parity treaty repeats each obligation with the roles of the two kings exchanged ('and for the other the same'); A long roster of the great gods and the gods of each city and land is named as present at the conclusion of the treaty.

Only in Sefire I face A - the treaty of Bar-Gaʾyah of KTK with Matiʿel of Arpad and the gods as witnesses (KAI 222 A 1-13): The gods El and Elyon are invoked as a pair; The witnessing gods are told 'open your eyes to look on the treaty'; The treaty is 'cut' (gzr), the Aramaic counterpart of cutting a covenant; The treaty is concluded before a long list of named gods, paired, ending with heaven and earth, abyss and springs, day and night; The treaty binds the kings, their sons, grandsons, offspring, nobles and whole lands.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: An oath by YHWH settles a dispute without witnesses (weight 7.7). Pair score 7.7.

Only in Šunaššura treaty, Hittite version (CTH 41.II.2): Mittani, help 'if it suits him', fugitives, wife and children as compensation: Whoever hides a fugitive in his house must give twelve persons in compensation, or himself be killed; a hiding slave's master may forfeit him; The vassal must not make peace or come to terms ('put his mouth') with the overlord's enemy; A parity treaty repeats each obligation with the roles of the two kings exchanged ('and for the other the same'); The overlord promises that if anyone presses the vassal, he himself, a prince or a great lord will come with troops and chariots and kill the enemy; Fugitives who flee from one realm to the other must be handed back; The sworn party must report any seditious or evil word heard against the king, whether from a brother, the king's own seed, an official, a friend or anyone, and must not conceal it.

Only in Covenant Code - theft, deposits, seduction: Liability for a borrowed animal that dies when the owner is absent; A dispute over deposited goods is brought before God (ha-elohim) for decision; A thief pays double; A thief who cannot pay is sold for his theft; A herdsman brings the remains of a torn animal as evidence and is not liable; Liability for one's grazing animals or spreading fire damaging another's field; Killing a burglar caught breaking in at night incurs no bloodguilt, but by day it does; A man who seduces an unbetrothed virgin must marry her or pay the bride-price; Who receives the marriage payment [divergence between the texts]; The penalty for theft [neutral] [contrast between the texts].

Only in CTH 52.I §11-12: the gods of Mittani; Šattiwazza and the Hurrians curse themselves - tamarisk, water of the gutter, smoke, salt; their blessing in the lord's shade: Self-curse: as salt has no seed, so may we have no seed; like a dissolved lump of salt may we not be restored; Self-curse: as a felled tree (tamarisk/acacia) puts out no shoot, so may we have no seed; Self-curse: may we rise like smoke to heaven; The vassal asks that the great king love him and his land as he loves his own lands, sons and his own tablet; The sworn people pray to eat a rich harvest in their lord's shade (ṣillu) while he goes before them; The sworn speak in the first person ('if we ...') and call on the named gods to seek out their seed if they rebel; Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nāsatyas are invoked as witnesses of a Mittani treaty; Treaty blessing: may the land be restored as of old, grow rich and lie down (rabāṣu) in peace; Treaty curse: may the gods overturn your throne; The vassal may keep concubines but may take no wife above or equal to the overlord's sister or daughter, who must be chief wife; The people and lands relax under the king's broad protection (an-dul3, 'shade'); Treaty blessing: if the vassal keeps the words written on the tablet, the oath gods guard him with his person, wives, sons, grandsons, house, city and land; and 2 more.

Only in Aid in revolt, feeding troops, captives, evil words and secret orders (CTH 62 §§12-16): If the king secretly orders something that cannot be done, the vassal must protest on the spot 'I cannot do this and I will not do it'; failing to do a feasible order breaks the oath; A secret word confided by the ruler must be kept; divulging it is a breach; Words the overlord tells the vassal in secret must be kept secret; revealing them breaks the oath; The overlord promises that if anyone presses the vassal, he himself, a prince or a great lord will come with troops and chariots and kill the enemy; A ruler who did not keep the treaty sworn by the gods is punished by them (defeat, death, abandonment); When an enemy rises or a revolt breaks out against the overlord, the vassal must go at once with his troops and chariots (or send his son or brother) to help; The sworn party must report any seditious or evil word heard against the king, whether from a brother, the king's own seed, an official, a friend or anyone, and must not conceal it.

Only in Aziru defends himself: do not listen to the false men who slander me; I was in Tunip, may your gods and the Sun know it (EA 161): A vassal says he provided for the overlord's envoy and carried him 'like a mother, like a father'; Slander or backbiting is pictured as eating the slandered person's flesh; Slanderers 'eat the pieces' (akālu karṣī) of the writer, maligning him before the king; A vassal reports to the overlord the news of neighbouring kings and rulers: deaths, successions, fires, alliances, hostilities; A vassal addresses the Egyptian king as 'my god(s), my Sun (god)'; Bowing to the ground seven times before a superior.

Only in Two Brothers: Bata's oath and self-castration; his heart to be placed on the cedar; Anubis kills his wife: Convinced of the hero's innocence, the husband goes home, kills his lying wife and throws her to the dogs; A mourner goes home with his hand on his head, which is smeared with dust (earth); The wronged man reproaches his kinsman: if you remember one bad thing, can you not remember one good thing I did for you?; The falsely accused man swears by the sun god, cuts off his own phallus with a reed knife and throws it into the water, where a catfish swallows it; A sign agreed in advance tells the brother of the hero's disaster: a jar of beer foams over and wine turns foul in his hand; Realising the wrong, the elder brother grieves and weeps aloud for his younger brother but cannot cross over to him; The hero takes out his heart and places it on the top of a tree; his life depends on it and he dies when the tree is felled; The dead hero's heart (found as a seed or grape after years of searching) is placed in a bowl of cool water; it drinks, he trembles, drinks it back and lives as before; What the husband does to the wife once her lie is known [neutral] [divergence between the texts]; On hearing bad news the hero sits, weeps, mourns and fasts for days; The husband recognizes his wife's guilt.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: The overlord has 'set his name' in a city (or at the rising and setting of the sun) for ever, so he cannot abandon it (weight 7.7); The vassal says it was not his father or mother but the strong arm of the king that set him in his father's house (weight 7.3); A vassal insists he is not a mere mayor (ḫazannu) but a soldier (weʾu) or companion of the king (weight 7.3); A letter ends with a note to the king's scribe asking him to present the writer's words eloquently to the king (weight 7.1); A ruler is 'not the son of his mother nor the son of his father' (weight 7.1); The vassal and his brothers are ready to die with (for) the king their lord (weight 6.5); An Akkadian letter uses or glosses a word with its Canaanite (West Semitic) equivalent (weight 4.5); Bandits or brigands called sa-gaz (Akkadian ḫabbātu, the Ḫabiru/ʿapiru) (weight 4.2); A vassal begs the overlord to send archers (piṭṭātu) quickly, or the city and land will be lost (weight 4.1); Bowing to the ground seven times before a superior (weight 3.1).
