Only in Abdi-Heba: the king has set his name at sunrise and sunset; I am a soldier, the king's companion; like a ship in the sea; rulers slain at the gate; we will die with the king (EA 288): The beleaguered vassal likens himself to a ship in the midst of the sea; A word of the root ḥ-n-p (Canaanite ḥanpa 'impious deed', Arabic ḥanīf) applied to a deed or a person [neutral] [divergence between the texts]; Who rules or commands the rising and the setting of the sun, in speech about a king [divergence between the texts]; Rulers are killed by their own towns or at the city gate, like dogs, and no one avenges them or the king does not ask after them; A king is murdered by his own servants in a conspiracy; The vassal longs to go to court and see the two eyes (the face) of the king, but enemies prevent him; Vassal declares 'I am your servant and your son' to an imperial king; A vassal sends people (girls, boys, servants) to the overlord as tribute; The king is to rule from the rising to the setting of the sun, from the upper to the lower sea; A vassal addresses the Egyptian king as 'my god(s), my Sun (god)'.

Only in Abdi-Heba: Milkilu and the sons of Labaya gave the king's land to the Habiru; the king is righteous to me; Cushites nearly killed me; my caravan was robbed in Ayyalon; the king has set his name in Jerusalem for ever (EA 287): The vassal declares 'the king my lord is righteous (ṣaduq) toward me'; The caravan carrying the vassal's tribute to the king is plundered in the fields on the way; A man with a bronze dagger stands over the ruler to kill him at an enemy's instigation; the ruler survives and slays him; The kings of the lands say to one another: come, let us go against the king; The overlord's letter orders a vassal to guard the king's place, obey the royal official and have bread, wine and supplies ready for the arriving troops.

Only in Eloquent Peasant (version B1): the second petition (the scales tilt, the officials are inverted): Theft is pardonable in the destitute, but not in the one who lacks nothing and is sated with bread and beer; Maat (justice) flees from under the judge, driven from her place; The great man is reminded that he will die with his dependants: will you be a man of eternity?; The judge should be a refuge, but his landing place is infested with crocodiles; The judge is invoked as the one who brings the drowning to shore and rescues the shipwrecked; The one who should see is blind, the one who should hear is deaf, the guide has become one who leads astray; Those with eyes and ears who neither see nor hear; The judge is admonished: do not speak falsehood, for you are great, weighty, the balance itself; The official is called the steering oar of heaven, the beam of the earth, the plumb-line that carries the weight; he must not swerve, tilt or waver; Rhetorical question whether a mortal will be one who lasts for ever; Catalogue of officials turned into their opposites: the distributor robs, the dispeller of need causes it, the harbour is a flood, the punisher of evil does wrong; Justice as a balance: the judge's tongue is the plummet, his heart the weight, his lips the arms of the scale; the scale must not tilt.

Only in Injustice, divine judgment, and humans no better than beasts: God tests humans to show them that they are but beasts; man has no advantage over the beast; Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes down to the earth?; God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter; Whether death is the end: asked, held by sceptics, or answered by resurrection [response between the texts]; Whether those who die and return to dust rise again [contrast between the texts]; Who will bring him to see what will be after him?; One fate (miqreh) befalls the wise and the fool, man and beast alike; Do evildoers think God will make them equal to the righteous in life and in death?; There is nothing better than to eat, drink and find enjoyment in one's toil; this is from the hand of God; Human comes from dust and returns to dust.

Only in The Seven goad Erra: the field is better than the city (Erra I 45-91): The open field is praised over city life: city bread cannot compare with a cake baked in embers, the palace with a shepherd's hut; Neglected weapons: cobwebs on the war gear, the bow too stiff, the arrowhead dull, the sword rusted for lack of slaughter; In a primeval or ideal land the lion does not kill and the wolf does not carry off the lamb; A warrior god lies idle in bed with his wife and is goaded by his weapons and companions to go out to war; Destruction motivated by human noise or overpopulation; Nations will beat swords into plowshares and spears into pruning hooks and learn war no more.

Only in David's thanksgiving psalm (composite of Pss 105, 96, 106): A psalm sung in the narrative is stitched from passages found in the Psalter; Prayer: 'save us, gather us and deliver us from the nations'; The patriarchs few in number wander from nation to nation, protected by God; All the people say 'Amen' and praise YHWH; 'Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm'; The world is firmly established and cannot be moved; Hymn recalls God's covenant with Abraham, oath to Isaac and statute to Jacob for a thousand generations; God comes to judge the earth with righteousness, and all creation rejoices; Proclamation among the nations: 'YHWH is king' (YHWH malakh); Idols called 'elilim' ('nothings'); YHWH is great and to be feared above all gods; Refrain 'Give thanks to YHWH for he is good, for his steadfast love is forever'.

Only in Esarhaddon chosen over his elder brothers; their revolt; his march on Nineveh (Esarhaddon 1 i 1 - ii 11): The king has his whole army leap across a broad river as if it were a ditch; After the father's fall the brothers rebel and butt each other like young goats for the kingship; The king gathers the guilty who incited the rebellion, punishes them and destroys their seed; The defeated rival princes abandon their troops and flee to an unknown land; The opposing troops declare 'this is our king' and go over to him; The war goddess stands at the king's side and breaks his enemies' bows; The gods remove the threatened heir to a secret place and spread their protection over him; The king sets out at once in the cold of winter without waiting a day or preparing his troops; Hearing of the revolt, the king cries 'woe', tears his princely garment and rages like a lion; Messages of ecstatic prophets (mahhû), sent by gods and goddesses, constantly reach and encourage the king; What the jealous brothers do, or plan, with their father's favour toward the chosen son [neutral] [divergence between the texts]; Jealous brothers spread slander and falsehood against the chosen heir and turn the father's heart against him; and 7 more.

Only in Jacob adopts and blesses Ephraim and Manasseh: Blessing formula 'May God make you like X and Y' coined by a patriarch; Children placed on or taken from the knees of a patriarch as an adoption gesture; Grandfather adopts two grandsons as his own sons, equal to his firstborn; Blessing that descendants teem like fish; The angel who redeemed the patriarch from all evil is invoked to bless; Patriarch bequeaths a portion (shekhem) he took from the Amorites with sword and bow; Grandfather crosses his hands to bless the younger first; The father's eyesight fails [divergence between the texts]; A dying father gathers his sons to bless them and foretell their destinies; Whether an adopted or fostered child counts as one's own child [contrast between the texts]; The father's eyesight fails; God called the patriarch's shepherd all his life.

Only in The pacified Delta and the wretched Asiatic, a crocodile on its bank (Instruction for Merikare): The old king tells how he pacified the west and settled the eastern border with towns of choice people to repel foreigners; Because the revenues of the north are in the king's hand, a failure of the Nile flood will not distress him; The king had the Asiatics struck, their people captured and their cattle seized until they abhorred Egypt; The Asiatic nomad is wretched: his land is short of water and wood, he never settles, fights 'since the time of Horus', neither wins nor is defeated, a crocodile on its bank.

Only in The boundaries of Judah: The 'Ascent of Scorpions' (Ma'aleh Aqrabbim) on the border; A spring called Ein Shemesh, 'spring of the sun'; A boundary stone named for Bohan son of Reuben; A valley named for the Rephaim near Jerusalem; The Valley of the son of Hinnom (later Gehenna) marks Jerusalem's border; Kiriath-jearim also called Baalah or Kiriath-baal; A tribe's boundary traced point by point; The land is apportioned to the tribes by casting lots before YHWH.

Only in Sud of Ereš; Enlil, without a wife, finds her, is rebuffed, and sends Nuska with a proposal (Enlil and Sud): A god or king without a wife travels through the land searching for a bride and chooses one for her beauty; A suitor's first, impertinent approach is rebuffed by the young woman, who goes into her house; At marriage the bride receives a new, exalted name ('the goddess without a name now has a famous name'); A minister is sent to the bride's mother with jewellery and a formal proposal of marriage on his master's behalf; The queen (shegal) sits beside the king as the courtier makes his request; God changes a person's name to mark a new destiny.

Only in Abraham's servant finds Rebekah for Isaac: God sends his angel ahead to guide the journey; The bride is asked and consents to go ('I will go'); Son brings bride into his dead mother's tent and is comforted; Patriarch goes out to meditate (or pray) in the field at evening; Hero asks God for a specific sign to identify the right person (who will offer water); Departing bride blessed to become thousands of myriads; Father insists his son's wife come from his own kin, not the local women; Bride covers herself with a veil on seeing the groom; On entering houses greet one another with a blessed greeting from God; Oath sworn by placing the hand under the thigh of the one demanding it; Descendants will possess the gate of their enemies; Believing women are to draw their outer cloaks (jalabib) over themselves so they are recognized and not harmed; and 5 more.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Hero stays three days and three nights in the belly of a fish or in the underworld (weight 7.7). Pair score 7.7.

Only in Ninšubur mourns and appeals; Enki creates the kur-ĝara and gala-tura (Inana's descent 173-253): A petitioner goes to three great gods in turn (Enlil, Nanna, Enki); the first two refuse and the third helps; A god creates new beings from the dirt under his fingernail; Created emissaries slip through the door like flies and the door pivots like phantoms; A mourner dresses in a single garment like a pauper and goes alone to the temple; Plea not to let precious silver, lapis lazuli and boxwood (the goddess) be ruined in the dust of the underworld; Offered a river and a field of grain, the envoys refuse every gift and ask only for the corpse; The queen of the underworld lies in pain over her children, uncovered, with dishevelled hair; A mourner sets up a lament on the ruin mounds, beats the drum in the sanctuary and makes the rounds of the gods' houses; Visitors echo the sufferer's groans ('Oh my heart' / 'oh your heart') and so win her oath to grant a favour; A life-giving plant and life-giving water that restore the dead to life; Mourners shave their heads, clip beards and gash their bodies; The underworld is the land of no return, the road whose traveller never comes back.

Only in Jonah swallowed by the great fish and his psalm: The speaker goes down to the roots (or cut-offs) of the mountains where the earth's bars close behind him forever; The speaker cries from 'the belly of Sheol' (beten sheol); The speaker is cast into the deep, the heart of the seas, with the current around him; The dying man remembers God and his prayer reaches God's holy temple; he looks again toward the temple; Declaration 'Salvation belongs to YHWH'; Reeds or seaweed (suf) are wrapped round the drowning man's head; Deep calls to deep at the roar of your water-spouts (tsinnorot); all your breakers pass over me; At God's command the fish vomits the prophet onto dry land [divergence between the texts]; God 'appoints' (wayeman) a series of natural agents: fish, plant, worm, wind; The man of the fish (Dhū l-Nūn) cries from the darknesses 'There is no god but you; I was a wrongdoer' and is saved [divergence between the texts]; God appoints a great fish to swallow the prophet; At God's command the fish vomits the prophet onto dry land; and 6 more.

Only in Inana passes the seven gates, is stripped, judged and hung on a hook (Inana's descent 68-172): The slain body is turned into a corpse and hung on a hook (peg) on the wall; At the gate of the netherworld the gatekeepers question those who arrive [divergence between the texts]; Before a perilous journey the deity instructs a faithful minister what to do if she does not return; The arriving goddess makes her sister rise from the throne and sits on it herself; Seven underworld judges give their verdict: their look is the look of death, their word the word of anger, their shout the shout of guilt; At each underworld gate one ornament or garment is removed until the goddess arrives naked; A figure slaps his or her thigh in dismay or grief on hearing bad news; The netherworld (hell) has seven gates; Arriving at a closed house or gate, a deity calls out to the doorkeeper by name: 'Open the house, open!'; Death or Sheol has gates (sha'arei mavet); Like a vanishing cloud, whoever goes down to Sheol does not come up; his place knows him no more.

Only in Nergal goes down, passes the seven gates and refuses all she offers (Nergal and Ereškigal, SB): The underworld queen orders the god who slighted her envoy brought before her (to die); One god alone does not stand or kneel before the underworld queen's envoy, an insult for which she demands him to be sent down to die; A god going down to the underworld is warned not to sit on the chair offered, eat its bread or meat, drink its beer, have his feet washed, or desire its queen when she bathes; The underworld as a land of darkness and deep shadow, without order, where light is like darkness; In the House of Dust the dead eat dust and clay, are clothed in feathers like birds and see no light; A messenger prostrates himself and kisses the ground before the deity he addresses.

Only in The marriage of Martu: the festival of Inab, Martu's wrestling victory, his refusal of silver and request for Numušda's daughter, and his marriage gifts: The victor refuses silver and precious stones and asks instead for the god's daughter in marriage; At a city festival the hero wrestles (ĝešba) in the great courtyard and fells all comers; The hero refuses each offered gift (wealth, weapons, plenty) in turn; A strong stranger is offered a reward by the girl's father and marries the daughter [divergence between the texts]; No hero, strongman or athlete of the lands can resist the king at wrestling and athletics; The marriage gifts sent to the bride's family are catalogued at length: herds, wild animals, cheeses, honey, fruits, metals, stones.

Only in Hymn to Nikkal-wa-Ib - the moon god Yarikh woos Nikkal, pays the bride-price, the family weighs it; the Kotharat (KTU 1.24): The bride's father, mother, brother and sister set up the scales and weigh the bride-price; The singer says the names of the goddesses are in his mouth, their count on his lips, and lists them; The bride's father suggests the suitor marry another (more prestigious) girl instead; The moon god burns with desire at sunset and embraces the maiden; The moon god is called 'the lamp of heaven' (nyr šmm) and asked to shine on the worshipper; The suitor refuses the alternative and insists on the bride he chose, and marries her; The divine suitor sends to the bride's father offering a bride-price of a thousand silver and ten thousand gold and lapis, and to turn her field into vineyards; The Kotharat, daughters of Hilal (the new moon), 'the swallows', goddesses of conception and birth, are feasted or invoked; To whom the bride-price is paid and in what (silver and gold to her father; service to her father; the gift to the woman herself) [divergence between the texts]; A poem opens with the singer's vow 'I will sing / praise the mighty one' followed by the hero's titles; The storm god's daughters (or brides) are Pidray daughter of light, Tallay daughter of showers (dew), Arṣay daughter of the wide earth; The high god El is 'the Bull, your father', 'the Kindly, the Compassionate (lṭpn il dpid)', 'Creator of creatures', 'father of years'.

Only in The marriage of Martu: gifts to the people of Inab, the friend's warning that Martu is an uncivilised nomad, and Adĝarkidug's answer 'I will marry Martu': A friend warns the girl against marrying an uncouth outsider, but she replies 'I will marry Martu'; The nomad is described as uncivilized: lives in tents in wind and rain, offers no prayer, digs truffles, does not bend the knee, eats raw meat, has no house in life and no burial at death; The desert nomad does not know the gods' place or God's limits, and does not pray; Invaders described as subhuman: human intelligence but dog's instincts and monkey's features, knowing no restraint; The marriage gifts sent to the bride's family are catalogued at length: herds, wild animals, cheeses, honey, fruits, metals, stones; A thing or conduct is declared an abomination (Sumerian niĝ2-gig, Akkadian ikkibu, Hebrew to'evah) to a god or king.

Only in The Rechabites refuse wine and are held up as a model of obedience: A family is promised that it will never lack a man to stand before God; A family's faithful obedience to its ancestor's command shames the people who disobey God; The Rechabites keep their ancestor's command never to drink wine; Nomads take refuge in Jerusalem from invading armies; A named chamber in the temple belonging to the sons of a 'man of God'; The prophet sets wine before abstainers in the temple and they refuse; Long life is promised if the king walks in God's ways; Nazirite abstains from wine, vinegar, grapes and everything from the vine down to seeds and skins; God sends his messengers 'rising early and sending' out of compassion.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: An outcry raised in the netherworld seizes and detains the living visitor (weight 7.1); Refrain: no demon, plague or battle took him, but the netherworld seized him (weight 6.8). Pair score 13.9.

Only in Enkidu seized, Gilgameš's lament and appeal to Enlil (Nibru recension 5.A): Seven days pass from the fateful day without the lost one returning; Every prohibition given is repeated as broken, item by item; A hero laments his beloved servant, faithful companion and counsellor; A hero goes alone to a god's temple and weeps out his petition.

Only in Enkidu breaks every taboo and the Netherworld seizes him (Gilgameš SB XII): The netherworld itself seizes and holds a living man; The dead recognise a living visitor as a stranger by his clean garments and scent; The queen of the netherworld lies uncovered, with pickaxe-like nails, tearing her hair; Rules for visiting the netherworld: no clean clothes, oil, sandals, weapons, shouting, or kissing and striking wife and son; The earth opens its mouth and swallows rebels alive into Sheol.

Only in Gods help the design; Gudea measures the site and moulds the first brick (Cyl. A 17.10-20.4): The king himself makes the first, 'fated' brick of the temple in a holy brick mould, amid music and ritual; A measuring line will be stretched over Jerusalem for rebuilding; David vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob not to enter his house or sleep until he found a place for YHWH; God fills craftsmen with a spirit of wisdom for sacred work; The sanctuary is built after a pattern shown by God on the mountain; The king's personal god goes with him and holds him by the hand.

Only in Altar rebuilt, Sukkot kept, foundation of the second temple laid amid weeping and shouting: Returnees rebuild the altar on its former foundations before the temple itself; Temple building begins in the second month, as Solomon's did; Burnt offerings resume from the first of the seventh month before the temple foundation is laid; Elders who saw the first temple weep aloud at the foundation of the second; The sound of joyful shouting cannot be distinguished from the sound of weeping; Levites serve from twenty years old and upward; The people gather 'as one man' to Jerusalem; Praise refrain 'for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever'; Seven-day festival of dwelling in booths recalling the wilderness; Cedars from Lebanon floated by sea to Joppa for the temple, paid with food and oil to Sidonians and Tyrians.

A 26.20-30.16): Seven stones set around the temple take counsel with its divine owner; Sparrow and swallow find a nest for their young at God's altars; The temple's kitchens, brewery, cow-pen and storehouses pour out butter, cakes and beer as abundant as the Tigris; Temple worship with cymbals, harps, lyres and priestly trumpets; In that day the mountains drip sweet wine and the hills flow with milk; Birds of every wing nest in the branches and shade of a great tree (kingdom); The fearsome radiance of the temple covers all lands like a garment; Figures of dragons, lions, wild bulls and other monsters guard the temple doors and gates; God stands or presides in the assembly of the gods (council of El, holy ones); A composition ends with a doxology to its deity: 'praise of X is sweet / magnificent' (za3-mi2).

Only in The prince's worship, gate rules, land gifts and temple kitchens: The inner east gate is shut on the six working days and opened on the sabbath and the new moon; A prince's gift of land to a servant reverts to him in the year of liberty (deror); Worshippers who enter by the north gate must leave by the south gate, and vice versa, not returning the way they came; The princes must not dispossess or oppress the people; they receive a fixed estate; Additional offerings for Sabbath and new moon; Perpetual offering of two lambs daily, morning and evening.

Only in Gudea tells his dream and Nanše interprets it (Cyl. A 4.14-6.13): A god appears as a figure as huge as heaven and earth, with a god's head, bird wings and a flood-storm for lower body, lions lying at his sides; The king himself makes the first, 'fated' brick of the temple in a holy brick mould, amid music and ritual; A god draws the ground plan of a temple on a lapis lazuli tablet; A goddess with a silver stylus consults a tablet of propitious stars to announce the time for building; David vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob not to enter his house or sleep until he found a place for YHWH; The sanctuary is built after a pattern shown by God on the mountain; Hero attributes his dream interpretation to God; Each figure and object of a symbolic dream is identified in turn by the interpreter (the man is X, the woman is Y).

Only in The book of remembrance and the sun of righteousness: The day comes burning like an oven; the arrogant and evildoers become stubble, left neither root nor branch; Complaint: 'It is vain to serve God; what profit that we kept his charge? The arrogant are blessed and the wicked test God and escape'; God will spare the faithful as a man spares the son who serves him, on the day he makes his treasured possession; The righteous go out leaping like stall-fed calves and tread the wicked like ashes under their feet; A book of remembrance is written before God for those who fear him and think on his name; God's choosing of Israel among the peoples [divergence between the texts]; There is no secret conversation of three but God is the fourth, nor of five but he is the sixth, wherever they are; God will not leave believers as they are until he separates the bad from the good; God's messengers (angels) write down what people plot and do; God records what people sent ahead and their traces (athar), and counts everything in a clear register (imam mubin); 'Why do the wicked live, grow old and mighty?': prosperity of the wicked with children, safe houses and fertile cattle; On judgment day people are either wretched (shaqi) or blessed (sa'id); and 3 more.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: God visits the earth with rain, softens it with showers, and crowns the year with harvest (weight 6.0); God celebrated as a warrior ('YHWH is a man of war') (weight 5.3). Pair score 11.3.

Only in Gudea's incubation and Ninĝirsu's self-revelation (Cyl. A 8.2-12.11): The god promises to touch the dreamer's arm with fire as a sign confirming his commission; A god recites his own titles, deeds, weapons and shrines in the first person ('I am ...'); The god comes and stands at the head of the sleeper, touches him and speaks; The god promises rain, full canals and rich harvests once the king builds his temple; The deity gives the one he commissions a sign on his arm or hand [divergence between the texts]; From the day the temple's foundation is laid, God promises to bless the harvest; God rebukes the sea and dries it up and makes all rivers fail; Bashan, Carmel and Lebanon wither; God's thoughts and ways are higher than human ways as the heavens are higher than the earth; Nations and kings come to Zion's light bringing their wealth, flocks and timber for the sanctuary; Foreign king (Hiram of Tyre) supplies cedar and cypress from Lebanon for the temple in exchange for food; God appears to the king in a dream at night at a sanctuary after sacrifice; An offering by fire is a pleasing odor to God; and 3 more.

Only in Psalm 68, let God arise; the rider of the clouds marches from Sinai to his mountain: God rebukes the beast of the reeds (Egypt as hippopotamus or crocodile) and the herd of bulls; Envoys come from Egypt and Cush (Ethiopia) stretches out its hands to God; God ascends on high leading captives and receiving gifts among men; God's chariots are myriads, thousands upon thousands; the Lord among them as at Sinai; God says he will bring back (enemies or people) from Bashan and from the depths of the sea; God rides in the heaven of heavens of old and utters his mighty voice; Many-peaked mountains (Bashan) look with envy at the mountain God chose for his dwelling; A dove's wings covered with silver and its pinions with yellow-green gold; When Shaddai scattered kings, it snowed on Zalmon; A great host of women heralds (mevasserot) announces the victory and women divide the spoil; Dogs lick the blood of the slain enemies (or of the wicked king); The guilty are known by their marks and seized by the forelocks and the feet; and 10 more.

Only in Kirugu 4: Ningal twice pleads with An and Enlil in the assembly, but their word does not change (Lament for Urim 136-171): A city goddess weeps before the high gods (An, Enlil) and begs them 'let my city not be destroyed, let its people not perish', but they do not change their word; An intercessor pleads with the divine to spare a city whose destruction is decreed; the decree is not turned back [divergence between the texts]; The great gods in council decree the destruction of a city and its land; The verdict of the divine assembly to destroy is declared irrevocable; The storm of YHWH's fury goes out and whirls on the head of the wicked; in the latter days you will understand it; The god's utterance cannot be changed or overturned; A Sumerian song divided into numbered kirugu sections, each followed by a ĝišgiĝal antiphon.

passages.text: טֻמְאָתָ֣הּ בְּשׁוּלֶ֗יהָ לֹ֤א זָֽכְרָה֙ אַחֲרִיתָ֔הּ וַתֵּ֣רֶד פְּלָאִ֔ים אֵ֥ין מְנַחֵ֖ם לָ֑הּ רְאֵ֤ה יְהוָה֙ אֶת עָנְיִ֔י כִּ֥י הִגְדִּ֖יל אוֹיֵֽב

(1:11) כָּל עַמָּ֤הּ נֶאֱנָחִים֙ מְבַקְּשִׁ֣ים לֶ֔חֶם נָתְנ֧וּ מחמודיהם מַחֲמַדֵּיהֶ֛ם בְּאֹ֖כֶל לְהָשִׁ֣יב נָ֑פֶשׁ רְאֵ֤ה יְהוָה֙ וְֽהַבִּ֔יטָה כִּ֥י הָיִ֖יתִי זוֹלֵלָֽה (1:12) ל֣וֹא אֲלֵיכֶם֮ כָּל עֹ֣בְרֵי דֶרֶךְ֒ הַבִּ֣יטוּ וּרְא֗וּ אִם יֵ֤שׁ מַכְאוֹב֙ כְּמַכְאֹבִ֔י אֲשֶׁ֥ר עוֹלַ֖ל לִ֑י אֲשֶׁר֙ הוֹגָ֣ה יְהוָ֔ה בְּי֖וֹם חֲר֥וֹן אַפּֽוֹ (1:13) מִמָּר֛וֹם שָֽׁלַח אֵ֥שׁ בְּעַצְמֹתַ֖י וַיִּרְדֶּ֑נָּה פָּרַ֨שׂ רֶ֤שֶׁת לְרַגְלַי֙ הֱשִׁיבַ֣נִי אָח֔וֹר נְתָנַ֨נִי֙ שֹֽׁמֵמָ֔ה כָּל הַיּ֖וֹם דָּוָֽה (1:14) נִשְׂקַד֩ עֹ֨ל פְּשָׁעַ֜י בְּיָד֗וֹ יִשְׂתָּֽרְג֛וּ עָל֥וּ עַל צַוָּארִ֖י הִכְשִׁ֣יל כֹּחִ֑י נְתָנַ֣נִי אֲדֹנָ֔י בִּידֵ֖י לֹא אוּכַ֥ל קֽוּם (1:15) סִלָּ֨ה כָל אַבִּירַ֤י אֲדֹנָי֙ בְּקִרְבִּ֔י קָרָ֥א עָלַ֛י מוֹעֵ֖ד לִשְׁבֹּ֣ר בַּחוּרָ֑י גַּ֚ת דָּרַ֣ךְ אֲדֹנָ֔י לִבְתוּלַ֖ת בַּת יְהוּדָֽה (1:16) עַל אֵ֣לֶּה אֲנִ֣י בוֹכִיָּ֗ה עֵינִ֤י עֵינִי֙ יֹ֣רְדָה מַּ֔יִם כִּֽי רָחַ֥ק מִמֶּ֛נִּי מְנַחֵ֖ם מֵשִׁ֣יב נַפְשִׁ֑י הָי֤וּ בָנַי֙ שֽׁוֹמֵמִ֔ים כִּ֥י גָבַ֖ר אוֹיֵֽב (1:17) פֵּֽרְשָׂ֨ה צִיּ֜וֹן בְּיָדֶ֗יהָ אֵ֤ין מְנַחֵם֙ לָ֔הּ צִוָּ֧ה יְהוָ֛ה לְיַעֲקֹ֖ב סְבִיבָ֣יו צָרָ֑יו הָיְתָ֧ה יְרוּשָׁלִַ֛ם לְנִדָּ֖ה בֵּינֵיהֶֽם (1:18) צַדִּ֥יק ה֛וּא יְהוָ֖ה כִּ֣י פִ֣יהוּ מָרִ֑יתִי שִׁמְעוּ נָ֣א כָל עמים הָֽעַמִּ֗ים וּרְאוּ֙ מַכְאֹבִ֔י בְּתוּלֹתַ֥י וּבַחוּרַ֖י הָלְכ֥וּ בַשֶּֽׁבִי (1:19) קָרָ֤אתִי לַֽמְאַהֲבַי֙ הֵ֣מָּה רִמּ֔וּנִי כֹּהֲנַ֥י וּזְקֵנַ֖י בָּעִ֣יר גָּוָ֑עוּ כִּֽי בִקְשׁ֥וּ אֹ֨כֶל֙ לָ֔מוֹ וְיָשִׁ֖יבוּ אֶת נַפְשָֽׁם (1:20) רְאֵ֨ה יְהוָ֤ה כִּֽי צַר לִי֙ מֵעַ֣י חֳמַרְמָ֔רוּ נֶהְפַּ֤ךְ לִבִּי֙ בְּקִרְבִּ֔י כִּ֥י מָר֖וֹ מָרִ֑יתִי מִח֥וּץ שִׁכְּלָה חֶ֖רֶב בַּבַּ֥יִת כַּמָּֽוֶת (1:21) שָׁמְע֞וּ כִּ֧י נֶאֱנָחָ֣ה אָ֗נִי אֵ֤ין מְנַחֵם֙ לִ֔י כָּל אֹ֨יְבַ֜י שָׁמְע֤וּ רָֽעָתִי֙ שָׂ֔שׂוּ כִּ֥י אַתָּ֖ה עָשִׂ֑יתָ הֵבֵ֥אתָ יוֹם קָרָ֖אתָ וְיִֽהְי֥וּ כָמֽוֹנִי (1:22) תָּבֹ֨א כָל רָעָתָ֤ם לְפָנֶ֨יךָ֙ וְעוֹלֵ֣ל לָ֔מוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר עוֹלַ֛לְתָּ לִ֖י עַ֣ל כָּל פְּשָׁעָ֑י כִּֽי רַבּ֥וֹת אַנְחֹתַ֖י וְלִבִּ֥י דַוָּֽי

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: The roads to Zion mourn because none come to the festivals (weight 6.8); The ruined city, personified as a woman, speaks in the first person (weight 6.6). Pair score 13.5.

Only in Kirugu 8: 'Lady, how can your heart endure?': priests, festivals and music gone; return to your city (Lament for Urim 331-389): In the ruined land there is no lament-singer left to perform the penitential lament; he has gone to foreign lands; The departed deity is begged to return to her city like an ox to its pen, a sheep to its fold, a young child to its chamber; The bricks of the ruined temple cry out like a person to the departed deity: 'Where are you?'; Temple personnel (cook, dream-interpreter, seal-keeper, linen-clad priests) are carried off and the rites forsaken; Prayer that the high god say 'It is enough!' and end the destruction; God turned the speaker's mourning into dancing, loosed his sackcloth and girded him with joy; The petitioner weeps to the god as to his own father and raises his hands; The city's own god stands outside his city as if it were an alien city; In the ruined temple the offerings, festivals, songs, drums and priestly offices cease; Desert creatures or demons (tsiyyim, iyyim) and ostriches inhabit the ruined city; Destruction undoes fertility: brackish water in rivers, weeds in fields, no lambs in the fold, no churning song; The noise of the city's songs and the sound of its lyres will be heard no more; and 5 more.

Only in Lamentations 1: 'How lonely sits the city', Zion as a widow with no comforter: The fallen city is likened to a menstruant (niddah) whose impurity is in her skirts; The ruined city sits alone like a widow; From on high God sent fire into the sufferer's bones; God spread a net for the sufferer's feet and turned him back; The Lord trod the virgin daughter of Judah as in a winepress; 'Is it nothing to you, all who pass by? Look and see if there is any sorrow like my sorrow'; Refrain that the city has no one to comfort her; The princes became like deer that find no pasture and flee without strength; The sufferer confesses 'YHWH is righteous, for I rebelled against his word'; The starving people trade their treasures for food to keep alive; The yoke of the sinner's transgressions is knotted by God's hand onto her neck; The sufferer's bowels churn and heart turns over within her; and 9 more.

Only in An, Enlil, Enki and Ninḫursaĝa decree the overthrow of Sumer and Urim (Sumer and Urim 1-57): The great gods in council decree the destruction of a city and its land; A city is granted kingship but not an eternal reign: every dynasty's turn must end; Captive king taken with hooks and bound in bronze fetters to Babylon; The roads to Zion mourn because none come to the festivals; God will silence the sound of joy and gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride; The chief god himself brings down a foreign people (Gutians, Elamites) from the mountains to destroy his land; Destruction undoes fertility: brackish water in rivers, weeds in fields, no lambs in the fold, no churning song; The storm of YHWH's fury goes out and whirls on the head of the wicked; in the latter days you will understand it; A destroyed city is made a perpetual ruin-mound (tel olam); 'Who can change the word that An, the king, has spoken?': the high god's decree cannot be altered.

Only in The great cedar of Eden felled and sent down to Sheol: The trees of Eden already in the netherworld are comforted when the great tree descends to join them; No tree in the garden of God, Eden, equalled the great tree's beauty; all the trees of Eden envied it; Assyria/Pharaoh as a towering cedar of Lebanon nourished by the deep (tehom), its top among the clouds, all birds nesting and beasts bearing young under it, all nations in its shade; God brings low the high tree and exalts the low tree, dries up the green tree and makes the dry tree flourish; The fallen king lies in the netherworld among the uncircumcised and those slain by the sword; Because it grew proud of its height, foreigners cut the great tree down; its boughs fall on mountains and valleys and the peoples leave its shade; Birds of every wing nest in the branches and shade of a great tree (kingdom); If God is silent the speaker will be like those who go down to the Pit (bor); God plants a garden (Eden) in the east and places the first human there; Oracle or vision dated by year, month and day of the exile of King Jehoiachin.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: The day of YHWH's anger on which none escape (weight 7.3); God himself spurns his altar and destroys his own sanctuary and festivals (weight 7.1). Pair score 14.4.

Only in The storm, the Gutians and the collapse of order; Ibbi-Suen weeps (Sumer and Urim 58-114): Corpses float in the river after the slaughter; The besieged king sits paralysed and weeps bitterly in his own palace; A catastrophe falls such as no one had ever known or seen, without a name; The crown has fallen from our head; woe to us for we have sinned; In the catastrophe a man turns away from wife, parents and children; In the catastrophe the father disowns his wife and the mother her child ('This is not my child'); Invaders fell every good tree, stop every spring and ruin every good field with stones; The chief god himself brings down a foreign people (Gutians, Elamites) from the mountains to destroy his land; City after city its god 'takes an unfamiliar path' away from his beloved dwelling and abandons it; God sends hail mingled with fire and thunder from heaven; The storm of YHWH's fury goes out and whirls on the head of the wicked; in the latter days you will understand it.

Only in Lamentations 2: the Lord became like an enemy; children faint in the streets: The city's ruin is as vast as the sea; who can heal it?; Infants and sucklings faint from hunger in the city squares, asking their mothers for bread and wine; Arise and cry out in the night at the beginning of the watches, pour out your heart like water; God did not remember his footstool (Zion or the ark) on the day of his anger; God cast down the splendor of Israel from heaven to earth; The mourner's liver is poured out on the ground; There is no torah, and the prophets find no vision from YHWH; Passers-by clap hands, hiss and wag their heads at the ruined city; Priest and prophet are slain in the sanctuary of the Lord; Enemies raise a shout in the temple as on a festival day; Let tears run down like a torrent day and night with no rest; The city's gates sink into the ground and their bars are broken; and 13 more.

Only in Complaint of the young men to Enki; Urim besieged; the queen led into slavery (Sumer and Urim 225-284): A god leaves his city like a prisoner of war, his hands fettered; Zion's precious sons, worth fine gold, now counted as clay pots; Lament cry: 'Why, YHWH, do you stand far off and hide in times of trouble?'; The city's goddess weeps bitterly: 'Alas, the destroyed city, my destroyed house'; Famine becomes severe in the besieged city; there is no bread; The chief god himself brings down a foreign people (Gutians, Elamites) from the mountains to destroy his land; City after city its god 'takes an unfamiliar path' away from his beloved dwelling and abandons it.

Only in Lamentations 1: 'How lonely sits the city', Zion as a widow with no comforter: The fallen city is likened to a menstruant (niddah) whose impurity is in her skirts; The ruined city sits alone like a widow; From on high God sent fire into the sufferer's bones; God spread a net for the sufferer's feet and turned him back; The Lord trod the virgin daughter of Judah as in a winepress; 'Is it nothing to you, all who pass by? Look and see if there is any sorrow like my sorrow'; Refrain that the city has no one to comfort her; The princes became like deer that find no pasture and flee without strength; The sufferer confesses 'YHWH is righteous, for I rebelled against his word'; The starving people trade their treasures for food to keep alive; The yoke of the sinner's transgressions is knotted by God's hand onto her neck; The sufferer's bowels churn and heart turns over within her; and 9 more.

(1:11) כָּל עַמָּ֤הּ נֶאֱנָחִים֙ מְבַקְּשִׁ֣ים לֶ֔חֶם נָתְנ֧וּ מחמודיהם מַחֲמַדֵּיהֶ֛ם בְּאֹ֖כֶל לְהָשִׁ֣יב נָ֑פֶשׁ רְאֵ֤ה יְהוָה֙ וְֽהַבִּ֔יטָה כִּ֥י הָיִ֖יתִי זוֹלֵלָֽה (1:12) ל֣וֹא אֲלֵיכֶם֮ כָּל עֹ֣בְרֵי דֶרֶךְ֒ הַבִּ֣יטוּ וּרְא֗וּ אִם יֵ֤שׁ מַכְאוֹב֙ כְּמַכְאֹבִ֔י אֲשֶׁ֥ר עוֹלַ֖ל לִ֑י אֲשֶׁר֙ הוֹגָ֣ה יְהוָ֔ה בְּי֖וֹם חֲר֥וֹן אַפּֽוֹ (1:13) מִמָּר֛וֹם שָֽׁלַח אֵ֥שׁ בְּעַצְמֹתַ֖י וַיִּרְדֶּ֑נָּה פָּרַ֨שׂ רֶ֤שֶׁת לְרַגְלַי֙ הֱשִׁיבַ֣נִי אָח֔וֹר נְתָנַ֨נִי֙ שֹֽׁמֵמָ֔ה כָּל הַיּ֖וֹם דָּוָֽה (1:14) נִשְׂקַד֩ עֹ֨ל פְּשָׁעַ֜י בְּיָד֗וֹ יִשְׂתָּֽרְג֛וּ עָל֥וּ עַל צַוָּארִ֖י הִכְשִׁ֣יל כֹּחִ֑י נְתָנַ֣נִי אֲדֹנָ֔י בִּידֵ֖י לֹא אוּכַ֥ל קֽוּם (1:15) סִלָּ֨ה כָל אַבִּירַ֤י אֲדֹנָי֙ בְּקִרְבִּ֔י קָרָ֥א עָלַ֛י מוֹעֵ֖ד לִשְׁבֹּ֣ר בַּחוּרָ֑י גַּ֚ת דָּרַ֣ךְ אֲדֹנָ֔י לִבְתוּלַ֖ת בַּת יְהוּדָֽה (1:16) עַל אֵ֣לֶּה אֲנִ֣י בוֹכִיָּ֗ה עֵינִ֤י עֵינִי֙ יֹ֣רְדָה מַּ֔יִם כִּֽי רָחַ֥ק מִמֶּ֛נִּי מְנַחֵ֖ם מֵשִׁ֣יב נַפְשִׁ֑י הָי֤וּ בָנַי֙ שֽׁוֹמֵמִ֔ים כִּ֥י גָבַ֖ר אוֹיֵֽב (1:17) פֵּֽרְשָׂ֨ה צִיּ֜וֹן בְּיָדֶ֗יהָ אֵ֤ין מְנַחֵם֙ לָ֔הּ צִוָּ֧ה יְהוָ֛ה לְיַעֲקֹ֖ב סְבִיבָ֣יו צָרָ֑יו הָיְתָ֧ה יְרוּשָׁלִַ֛ם לְנִדָּ֖ה בֵּינֵיהֶֽם (1:18) צַדִּ֥יק ה֛וּא יְהוָ֖ה כִּ֣י פִ֣יהוּ מָרִ֑יתִי שִׁמְעוּ נָ֣א כָל עמים הָֽעַמִּ֗ים וּרְאוּ֙ מַכְאֹבִ֔י בְּתוּלֹתַ֥י וּבַחוּרַ֖י הָלְכ֥וּ בַשֶּֽׁבִי (1:19) קָרָ֤אתִי לַֽמְאַהֲבַי֙ הֵ֣מָּה רִמּ֔וּנִי כֹּהֲנַ֥י וּזְקֵנַ֖י בָּעִ֣יר גָּוָ֑עוּ כִּֽי בִקְשׁ֥וּ אֹ֨כֶל֙ לָ֔מוֹ וְיָשִׁ֖יבוּ אֶת נַפְשָֽׁם (1:20) רְאֵ֨ה יְהוָ֤ה כִּֽי צַר לִי֙ מֵעַ֣י חֳמַרְמָ֔רוּ נֶהְפַּ֤ךְ לִבִּי֙ בְּקִרְבִּ֔י כִּ֥י מָר֖וֹ מָרִ֑יתִי מִח֥וּץ שִׁכְּלָה חֶ֖רֶב בַּבַּ֥יִת כַּמָּֽוֶת (1:21) שָׁמְע֞וּ כִּ֧י נֶאֱנָחָ֣ה אָ֗נִי אֵ֤ין מְנַחֵם֙ לִ֔י כָּל אֹ֨יְבַ֜י שָׁמְע֤וּ רָֽעָתִי֙ שָׂ֔שׂוּ כִּ֥י אַתָּ֖ה עָשִׂ֑יתָ הֵבֵ֥אתָ יוֹם קָרָ֖אתָ וְיִֽהְי֥וּ כָמֽוֹנִי (1:22) תָּבֹ֨א כָל רָעָתָ֤ם לְפָנֶ֨יךָ֙ וְעוֹלֵ֣ל לָ֔מוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר עוֹלַ֛לְתָּ לִ֖י עַ֣ל כָּל פְּשָׁעָ֑י כִּֽי רַבּ֥וֹת אַנְחֹתַ֖י וְלִבִּ֥י דַוָּֽי

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: A lament opens with the cry 'Eikhah!' (How!) (weight 7.1); The roads to Zion mourn because none come to the festivals (weight 6.8); The ruined city, personified as a woman, speaks in the first person (weight 6.6). Pair score 20.5.

Only in How did Nibru become haunted? When will it be restored? (Nibru 1-52): The Lord has become like an enemy to his own people; In the ruined city the seat of judgment stands empty and no decisions or justice are given; 'My lyre is turned to mourning and my pipe to the voice of weepers'; Desert creatures or demons (tsiyyim, iyyim) and ostriches inhabit the ruined city; Israel called the flock of God's pasture; Lament question 'How long, O God?' / 'Why have you rejected us forever?'.

Only in Lamentations 1: 'How lonely sits the city', Zion as a widow with no comforter: The fallen city is likened to a menstruant (niddah) whose impurity is in her skirts; The ruined city sits alone like a widow; From on high God sent fire into the sufferer's bones; God spread a net for the sufferer's feet and turned him back; The Lord trod the virgin daughter of Judah as in a winepress; 'Is it nothing to you, all who pass by? Look and see if there is any sorrow like my sorrow'; Refrain that the city has no one to comfort her; The princes became like deer that find no pasture and flee without strength; The sufferer confesses 'YHWH is righteous, for I rebelled against his word'; The starving people trade their treasures for food to keep alive; The yoke of the sinner's transgressions is knotted by God's hand onto her neck; The sufferer's bowels churn and heart turns over within her; and 8 more.

Only in The gods fashion the monstrous destroyer; who did this to Unug? (Lament for Unug, kirugu 1): Several great gods together create and give features and limbs to a monstrous destroying being; A destroying creature like a great wild bull bellows and its gigantic horns reach up to heaven; Mortal humans multiply until they are as numerous as the gods, preceding a divine decision to destroy; A lament piles up rhetorical questions: who did this to the city, why did the god's hand seize it, why did the kind eye look away; The city's patron god and its protective spirits (udug, lamma) leave it, flee to the open country and take foreign paths before its destruction; The great gods themselves blanch in fear at the immensity of a creature the gods have made; God stands or presides in the assembly of the gods (council of El, holy ones).

Only in 'Remember me'; Enkidu lies sick twelve days, lamenting he does not die in battle (Gilgameš SB VII): The dying hero lies sick day after day, counted from the first to the twelfth; The dying hero laments that he dies on a sickbed, not gloriously in battle where one makes a name; Leader prays 'remember me, my God, for good' for his deeds; Refrain: no demon, plague or battle took him, but the netherworld seized him.

Only in Enlil's deluge-monster; the foolish rejoice, the wise lament (Lament for Unug, kirugu 2-3): A destroying storm-monster sent by the god is described part by part: hair, face, eyes, mouth, tongue, arms, ribs, haunches, feet, each a weapon or fire; When doom is announced the foolish rejoice and look forward to war, while the wise beat their breasts, weep at night and cannot sleep; In the disaster honest men among loyal families turn into liars and traitors; Those threatened pray that the god's decree 'be turned back' and his anger be exhausted; Prayer that those who seized Enlil's temple (the E-kur) and coveted Nibru be punished and swept away; The Tigris and Euphrates quake and the mountains rumble before the divine onslaught; The sufferer floods his bed with tears every night; Monster's sneezes flash light, torches and sparks leap from its mouth, smoke from its nostrils; The god's decreed destruction is a 'deluge' (amaru, abubu) or storm that sweeps over the land, used of invading armies; A Sumerian song divided into numbered kirugu sections, each followed by a ĝišgiĝal antiphon.

Only in The Song of Moses (Ha'azinu): God refrains from annihilating Israel lest the enemy boast it was their own hand; God will provoke Israel to jealousy with a no-people, a foolish nation; Jeshurun grew fat and kicked, forsaking the God who made him; Nations called to rejoice as God avenges his servants' blood and atones for his land; God as the Rock that bore you and the God who writhed in labor with you; Teaching falls like rain and distils like dew; Their vine is from the vine of Sodom; grapes of poison, wine of serpents' venom; God is the father who acquired, made and established his people; God as purchaser of his people [divergence between the texts]; God raises his hand to heaven and swears: as I live forever; Whether God, or the gods, eat the offerings [contrast between the texts]; God nursed Israel with honey from the rock and oil from flint; and 30 more.

Only in Alas Sumer! The word of An and Enlil, Gutium and Subir sack the land (Lament for Unug, kirugu 4): The enemy 'puts out both eyes' of the city and uproots its young shoots (its people, its future); Kulaba (Unug) is called the primeval city, yet is turned into a place of murder; Experienced warriors drop their weapons, their minds confused, and their leaders are cut down; An invading people pours over the land like a swelling floodwave; The singer says 'my heart is filled with tears' in a refrain; Lament cry 'Alas, Sumer! Alas its people!' (a ki-en-gi) addressing the land itself; The enemy kills the population, young and old alike; A barbarian mountain people (Gutium, Subir, Martu) is the instrument of the gods' destruction of Sumer; The word or pronouncement of the high gods (An, Enlil) is itself the force that destroys the city; The god's decreed destruction is a 'deluge' (amaru, abubu) or storm that sweeps over the land, used of invading armies; A conquered city is burned with fire; A destroyed city is made a perpetual ruin-mound (tel olam).

Only in Maher-shalal-hash-baz; waters of Shiloah; the stone of stumbling; ghosts that chirp: The land of Zebulun and Naphtali, 'Galilee of the nations' by the way of the sea, first humbled and later glorified; The people reject the gently flowing waters of Shiloah, so God brings the mighty River (Assyria) to flood them up to the neck; Refrain 'Immanuel / for God is with us' against plotting nations; The prophet and the children God gave him are signs and portents in Israel; Prophet goes in to 'the prophetess' (his wife) who bears a sign-child; God becomes a sanctuary and a stone of stumbling and rock of offense, a trap and snare to both houses of Israel; Bind up the testimony, seal the teaching among my disciples; the prophet waits for the God who hides his face; Before a child knows to refuse evil and choose good (or say 'father, mother') the enemy kings' lands will be deserted; Ghosts and familiar spirits 'chirp and mutter'; 'should a people consult the dead on behalf of the living?'; Earlier messengers were given wives and offspring; Prophet's child bears a symbolic name that is itself an oracle (Shear-yashuv, Maher-shalal-hash-baz); Prophet commanded to write the oracle on a tablet and in a book as a witness for the last day, forever; and 2 more.

O the destroyed house!'; The destroying storm covers the city like a cloak and is spread over it like a linen sheet; A god weeps bitter tears over the destruction of his own city; The city's own god stands outside his city as if it were an alien city; A Sumerian song divided into numbered kirugu sections, each followed by a ĝišgiĝal antiphon.

Only in Ur-Namma's sickness, death and the road to the netherworld (Death of Ur-Namma): The king's donkeys and chariot are buried with him; The king's appointed day arrives and he dies in his prime; The netherworld is called Arali (or kur, irigal), where the dead king is brought; The dying king lies sick: his hands cannot grasp, his feet cannot step, he cannot raise his neck; The high god does not say 'enough' (stop the evil), and the king's days are not filled; The dead king is a boat sunk in a land foreign as Dilmun, stripped of oars, poles and rudder; The fallen king is a felled cypress, boxwood or cedar against which axes are set; The pious king's sacrifices and gifts are no longer accepted by the gods; The journey to the netherworld is a desolate road on which no one goes up and down; The sufferer is forgotten like a dead man, like a broken (lost) vessel; Like a vanishing cloud, whoever goes down to Sheol does not come up; his place knows him no more.

Only in Go down to the king's house - justice or ruin: God promises a lasting dynasty ('sure house') on condition of obedience; Passersby will be appalled and hiss at the ruined temple and ask why God did this; the answer is apostasy; God swears by himself.

Only in Ur-Namma's gifts to the netherworld gods and his installation as judge (Death of Ur-Namma): The food of the netherworld is bitter and its water brackish; The newly dead king slaughters bulls and sheep and seats the dead at a great banquet; The dead king is seated on a dais in the netherworld and with Gilgameš renders its judgments; the slain and the guilty are given into his hands; The dead king presents gifts to the seven chief porters and to each netherworld deity in their palaces; Namtar, the netherworld deity of fate, 'decrees all the fates'; The food and the drink of the netherworld (hell): bitter food, foul water [divergence between the texts]; Gilgameš is king and judge in the netherworld; Death or Sheol has gates (sha'arei mavet).

Only in Enkidu's dream of the House of Dust (Gilgameš SB VII): In the netherworld the crowns of former kings lie heaped away while the kings sit as servants; The dying man is struck and turned into a bird (dove), his arms bound like wings, and led to the netherworld; Before the queen of the netherworld her scribe crouches, reading a tablet aloud; she asks who brought the new arrival; A man dreams that a grim figure with a monstrous bird's face, lion's paws and eagle's talons seizes him, foreboding his death; In a dream the heavens roar, the earth rumbles, darkness falls, lightning flashes and death rains down until the fire goes out and turns to ash; In the House of Dust the dead eat dust and clay, are clothed in feathers like birds and see no light; Human comes from dust and returns to dust; The underworld is the land of no return, the road whose traveller never comes back.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Namtar, the netherworld deity of fate, 'decrees all the fates' (weight 7.7). Pair score 7.7.

Only in Ur-Namma's gifts to the netherworld gods and his installation as judge (Death of Ur-Namma): The food of the netherworld is bitter and its water brackish; The newly dead king slaughters bulls and sheep and seats the dead at a great banquet; The dead king is seated on a dais in the netherworld and with Gilgameš renders its judgments; the slain and the guilty are given into his hands; Famous dead kings and dead priests in the netherworld announce the newcomer's arrival and a tumult arises; The dead king presents gifts to the seven chief porters and to each netherworld deity in their palaces; A goddess is the chief scribe of the netherworld, given stylus, measuring line and rod; Sheol below is stirred to meet the arriving tyrant; the shades and dead kings rise from their thrones to greet him: 'you too have become weak like us'; The food and the drink of the netherworld (hell): bitter food, foul water [divergence between the texts]; Gilgameš is king and judge in the netherworld; Death or Sheol has gates (sha'arei mavet).

Only in Udug-hul compendium (STT 2 173): Namtar and the evil messengers; Ea's remedy of a clay substitute figure taken to the steppe before Šamaš: A bird (dove) of heaven is released and the direction of its flight, toward sunrise or sunset, is taken as an omen; The demons are 'evil messengers' (mārū šipri lemnūtu) who attack the land, fill it like locusts and lay sickness on man; At dawn the substitute figure is carried out to the steppe before the sun god, given provisions in a leather bag and set at the root of a thornbush facing sunset; Closing wish: may the evil demon stand aside and the good protective spirits (šēdu, lamassu) be present; The illness is hidden: no one knows its inside, and its poison cannot be seen; Asalluhi (Marduk) sees the affliction and reports it to his father Ea, who answers 'what I know you know; go, my son' and prescribes the ritual; A gag or affliction keeps food and drink from the sufferer's mouth; The washing water from the speaker's body and hands carries the evil onto a substitute figurine (ṣalam nigsagilê) which bears his sin in his place; street and way undo his sins; Augury: a bird's flight or alighting is an omen bound to a person [divergence between the texts]; The dead cannot go back to the life they left; The underworld is the land of no return, the road whose traveller never comes back.

Only in Oholah and Oholibah, the two harlot sisters: Having slaughtered their children to idols, they enter God's sanctuary the same day to profane it; The sisters' harlotry began in their youth in Egypt where their breasts were pressed; Egyptian paramours described with 'flesh of donkeys and issue of stallions'; Seeing men portrayed on a wall in vermilion (images of Chaldeans with belts and turbans), the woman lusts and sends messengers to them; The harlot lusts after Assyrian governors and officers clothed in blue, all handsome young horsemen; The adulteress's nose and ears are cut off as punishment; Two sisters, Oholah ('her tent') and Oholibah ('my tent is in her'), daughters of one mother, are Samaria and Jerusalem, wives of God who play the harlot; Enemy peoples named Pekod, Shoa and Koa come with the Babylonians and Assyrians; Drunkards (sove'im/Sabeans) brought from the desert put bracelets on the women's hands and crowns on their heads; The younger sister must drink her sister's deep and wide cup of horror and desolation, drain it, gnaw its sherds and tear her breasts; All women will be warned by the punishment of the lewd sisters and not imitate them; An assembly stones the adulteress and hacks her with swords and burns her houses before many women; and 5 more.

Only in Amar-Suena A: the temple of Enki left in ruins year after year, rebuilt only when Enki speaks: The king exchanges his royal garments for mourning clothes; The king searches for the god's plan (ĝiš-ḫur) for the temple and cannot find it until the god speaks; The people turn against (revolt from) the king during his building or reign; 'At that time' humanity had no wisdom or wise words and evil was thought good; Deeds are done or praised so that the praise is handed down to distant days and never forgotten; Year after year the temple lies in ruins until the king may rebuild it, the years counted one by one; The king performs extispicy before building a temple, and the omen withholds approval; The king, living in a cedar palace, proposes to build a house for God; The sanctuary is built after a pattern shown by God on the mountain; A god formally decrees (nam tar) a good destiny for the king: heroism, long reign, splendour.

Only in Cedar paneling, gold, the inner sanctuary and the cherubim: Two cherubim of olive wood, ten cubits high, whose outstretched wings span the inner sanctuary wall to wall; The inner sanctuary (devir) is a perfect cube of twenty cubits overlaid with pure gold; Temple walls and doors are carved with cherubim, palm trees and open flowers, overlaid with gold; Archaic (Canaanite/Phoenician) month names Ziv, Bul and Ethanim are used; A small gold-plated altar for burning incense before the veil; The innermost room, the holy of holies, holds the ark; Exact dimensions of the temple building and its rooms are given in cubits; Two golden cherubim face each other with wings spread over the ark.

Only in Syncretistic Hymn to Marduk 18-60: 'Your name is Anšar ... Dagan ... Adad ... Šamaš ... your name is indeed Marduk': Syncretistic litany: each great god (Anšar, Dagan, Adad, Nannar, Šamaš, Erra, Ningirsu) is declared to be a name or aspect of the one supreme god: 'your name is X ... your name is indeed Marduk'; The supreme god alone holds the rope (ṣerretu) or bond of heaven and earth, his sceptre laid across the netherworld; YHWH rides on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; Egypt's idols tremble before him; How thunder in the clouds relates to the god: his own roar or a creature praising him [shared matter] [divergence between the texts]; Whatever name is pronounced, it belongs to the one god: 'he is our god' / 'his are the beautiful names' [divergence between the texts]; The god is creator of everything, without whom nothing whatsoever was formed and no lord could exist; The god's command cannot be altered and his assent cannot be changed; The god (alone) holds the heavens (and earth) in place: the bond or rope of heaven, holding back the sky; At the storm god's roar from the clouds heaven and earth shake, mountains quake and the seas are stirred up; Each line of a litany is repeated for one god under several names (Ninurta, Pabilsaĝ, Ninĝirsu), identifying them; The gods come and prostrate themselves before the victorious warrior god and greet him; The sun god is the king of justice who illuminates the land like a torch and assures the king's just rule; and 2 more.

Only in Syncretistic Hymn to Marduk 18-60: 'Your name is Anšar ... Dagan ... Adad ... Šamaš ... your name is indeed Marduk': Syncretistic litany: each great god (Anšar, Dagan, Adad, Nannar, Šamaš, Erra, Ningirsu) is declared to be a name or aspect of the one supreme god: 'your name is X ... your name is indeed Marduk'; The supreme god alone holds the rope (ṣerretu) or bond of heaven and earth, his sceptre laid across the netherworld; YHWH rides on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; Egypt's idols tremble before him; How thunder in the clouds relates to the god: his own roar or a creature praising him [shared matter] [divergence between the texts]; Whatever name is pronounced, it belongs to the one god: 'he is our god' / 'his are the beautiful names' [divergence between the texts]; The god is creator of everything, without whom nothing whatsoever was formed and no lord could exist; The god's command cannot be altered and his assent cannot be changed; The god (alone) holds the heavens (and earth) in place: the bond or rope of heaven, holding back the sky; At the storm god's roar from the clouds heaven and earth shake, mountains quake and the seas are stirred up; Each line of a litany is repeated for one god under several names (Ninurta, Pabilsaĝ, Ninĝirsu), identifying them; The gods come and prostrate themselves before the victorious warrior god and greet him; Cluster of divine epithets in sequence (e.g. the Forgiving, the Loving, Lord of the Throne, the Glorious, doer of what he wills; or Lord, King, God of mankind); and 1 more.

Only in Ištar ritual - braziers, bulls, cakes danced on the table, 'Ištar lady of heaven' sung: Kamānu-cakes are made to 'dance' (raised and moved) on the table before the deity; A purifying device (ša-tēlissi, torch) is passed over the offering table, the middle of the house and the censers to cleanse them; Aromatic wood (emdu) is thrown on the censer a fixed number of times (twice, three times) before the god; At each offering the officiant sings a named hymn to the deity concerned; Inana is titled lady, queen or mother of heaven (nin/ama an-na, 'queen of heaven'); The king himself performs the temple rite: he sets the table, strews salt, slaughters the sheep and completes the libation.

Only in A god given a golden throne, a fifty-headed mace and fifty names in Nibru; Išme-Dagan provisioner of Nibru and king of Isin (Išme-Dagan AA): The king makes and installs splendid thrones for the god and his consort in the temple and seats them there; The king is styled by his service to each great cult city in turn: provisioner of Nibru, attendant of Urim, the one who stands daily for Eridug, en of Unug, king of Isin; A temple gate (the lion-faced gate) is the place where fates are determined; A divine warrior lists his personified, named weapons (Mows-down-a-myriad, Crushes-a-myriad, the fifty-headed mace ...); Kingship is carried from city to city as each in turn is defeated in battle; Prayer that the king serve as the deity's steward and bring bulls, offerings, beer, fat, oil, syrup and wine.

Only in Enūma eliš VI (STT 1, 9): humankind bears the gods' toil; gods build Esagil; the bow; Marduk's names: The victorious god's bow is kissed by the high god, given names and set in the sky as a constellation; Seven gods of destinies are appointed in the assembly to decide fates; The god is the shining 'son, the sun of the gods', in whose bright light the gods walk for ever; What the god does in heaven is to be done likewise on earth: the earthly cult is the image (tamšīlu) of the heavenly; Formula: 'Ea created you, Ea unmade you' (the maker undoes what he made); The grateful gods mould bricks for a year and build Babylon and the temple Esagil with its ziggurat for their king; The gods swear allegiance with water and oil, touching their throats and invoking a curse on themselves; At creation heaven, earth and underworld are apportioned to three gods (An, Enlil, Ereškigala); At the temple's inauguration the high gods are seated in order of honour at a banquet; What humans were created for: to labour for and feed the gods, or to worship [divergence between the texts]; Humankind is created as a substitute to take over the gods' toil and carry their work-basket; Humanity or the Sumerians called 'the black-headed'.

Only in Inana, holder of the plans of kingship, leads Ur-Ninurta humbly into E-kur and speaks for him to An and Enlil; his shepherdship and throne are fixed (Ur-Ninurta A 1-43): A goddess brings the king, clasping a white lamb to his breast, into the chief god's temple and asks the god to decree his fate and call his name; The god's terrifying radiance (ni2, me-lem4) fills heaven and earth; The high god looks among the multitude of people and chooses the king to be his shepherd; The people and lands relax under the king's broad protection (an-dul3, 'shade'); Israel called the flock of God's pasture; Inana is titled lady, queen or mother of heaven (nin/ama an-na, 'queen of heaven'); The chief god gives the king shepherdship over the whole land, south and highlands; The god makes the king's throne firm so that no one can remove it; The king is made to rise over the land like the sun god; The king does justice and righteousness for all his people; A Sumerian song divided into numbered kirugu sections, each followed by a ĝišgiĝal antiphon.

Only in Assurbanipal's hymn to Aššur (SAA 3 1): The god is creator of those of heaven and earth, fashioner of the mountains and creator of the gods; A hymn opens with the singer's resolve: 'let me magnify the god, make his greatness manifest, extol his name'; A deity is 'wide of ear' and knows everything; All the Igigi kneel before the god and the Anunnaki praise his name from their sanctuaries; God's righteousness will be told to a people yet unborn; The warrior god (Ninurta, or Nabû in commentary) defeats and kills the Anzu bird; The god's ingenuity is like tangled threads no eye can follow; he is his own counsellor and no one comprehends his deeds.

Only in Iškur the storm-lord, shade of Larsa and helper in battle; Sîn-iddinam restores Eridug's plans and makes Iškur a great throne with two bulls (Sîn-iddinam E): The king fashions a great throne for the storm god, seats him on it, and sets beside it two great bull figures to gore the king's enemies right and left; The king is styled by his service to each great cult city in turn: provisioner of Nibru, attendant of Urim, the one who stands daily for Eridug, en of Unug, king of Isin; The king gathers the god's divine powers, attends to the ancient ordinances and restores the rites that had fallen out of use; Because of the king An gives rain and the gods give floods, grain and abundance; The people and lands relax under the king's broad protection (an-dul3, 'shade'); A god (Enki) gives the king broad understanding and knowledge of everything; The king sets up his own statue before the god so that his fame endures; The king's personal god goes with him and holds him by the hand; God appears in storm: clouds pour, his arrows (lightning) fly, thunder rolls in the whirlwind.

Only in Sippar cylinder: Ehulhul rebuilt on Ashurbanipal's foundation; Sîn's return and prayer (Nabonidus 28 i 34-ii 46): The king musters labour from the border of Egypt (Gaza) and the Upper Sea to the Lower Sea to build the temple; Rebuilding a temple, the king digs down until he finds the foundation deposit of an ancient king and builds exactly on it; The bricks or mortar of the temple are mixed with oil, honey, ghee, wine and beer; Divine words read in a sheep's entrails decide purifications, the choice of priestesses and priests, and campaigns; The temple is likened to the new moon (crescent) shining in the sky; The heroes fell the tallest cedar, whose top touched heaven, and make a great door for the high god's temple, floated downriver by raft; A future king who restores the building is to find the inscription, anoint it with oil, sacrifice and return it to its place; After the decree of restoration the god re-enters his city and temple with head held high.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: God stirs up the spirit of foreign peoples against a sinful king (weight 7.7). Pair score 7.7.

Only in Letter from Ibbi-Suen to Puzur-Šulgi hoping for Išbi-Erra's downfall: The assembly of the gods and the land are dispersed; The high god turns against the land and raises a foreign upstart, not of native seed (an 'ape from the mountains'), to kingship; Governors of the king's cities defect to a rising rival, as the god's word has decreed; The great gods in council decree the destruction of a city and its land; Invaders described as subhuman: human intelligence but dog's instincts and monkey's features, knowing no restraint; The king rebukes an official: 'This is what I ordered you; why have you not done as I said?'; A letter closes with 'May my lord know!' or 'It is urgent!'; A letter opens with the formula 'Say to my lord (X): thus says Y, your servant' (or, from the king, 'thus says your lord').

Only in Jehoram kills his brothers; Elijah's letter; death by bowel disease, unlamented: A wicked king is struck with an incurable disease and his bowels come out; The wicked king dies and departs 'with no one's regret'; God will not destroy David's house, having promised him a lamp (nir) forever; On accession the new king kills all his brothers; The people make no funeral burning for a wicked king as for his fathers; Raiders carry off the king's wealth, wives and sons, leaving only the youngest; A subject people revolts and sets up its own king; The king does evil because he married a daughter of a wicked dynasty; A prophet sends a king a letter of judgment; The king distributes his sons among the fortified cities with provisions; A king's disaster is explicitly explained as immediate punishment for a specific sin.

Only in Hymn to the Sun god, opening epithets (CTH 372 §1-4): The sun god provides the gods, including the old (primeval) gods of the dark earth, with their offerings and portions; The gods of heaven and the deep bow down and kiss the feet of the supreme deity; The sun god is father and mother of the wronged and orphaned and makes good their case; God gathers the dispersed from the four corners (kanfot, 'wings') of the earth; The door of heaven is opened for the sun god and he strides through the gate of heaven; God is father of orphans and defender of widows, who sets the lonely in a home and frees prisoners; A god or king is adorned with a lapis-lazuli beard.

Only in Letter-prayer of Kug-Nanna to the god Ninšubur: in fetters, facing death abroad, ignored in the street; soothe your angry heart, drive out the demon, brighten my dark days: The petitioner begs that his bones not be carried off to a foreign city, i.e. that he not die in exile; A captive is put in foot-stocks, hand-stocks and a neck-stock and threatened with copper spikes; Prayer that the high god say 'It is enough!' and end the destruction; Friends and companions stand aloof from the sufferer's plague (nega); kin stand far off; A star or moon deity's radiance lights up the dark place where the sufferer lies; A deity is the minister (sukkal) of the high god, holding a lapis sceptre and walking before him; A king or individual writes a letter to a god, with the epistolary formula, setting out distress and asking for help (letter-prayer); Named demons (udug, lamma, Dimme, Namtar, Asag) beset mankind, entering by night and not leaving a man alone.

Only in 'Out of Egypt I called my son'; God's compassion overturns his anger: Admah and Zeboiim, destroyed with Sodom, cited as the fate God refuses to inflict; God taught Ephraim to walk, took them in his arms and drew them with cords of love; God roars like a lion and his children come trembling back from the west, Egypt and Assyria like birds and doves; 'When Israel was a child I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son'; God calls Israel 'my firstborn son' and threatens the oppressor's firstborn; Punishment is a return to Egypt (reversal of the exodus).

Only in Hymn to Asarluḫi (Marduk), firstborn of Enki: the river ordeal refines the just like gold; the god of incantation, pure hands and pure feet; settled in Kuara: An incantation of the sun god that even the great gods do not know; The wise god (Enki) is praised as great farmer, carpenter, sage (abgal) and master of purification rites; A deity renders verdicts and decrees judgments (di kud); A god calls himself the firstborn son of the supreme god; A song opens with the singer's announcement 'I will sing the song of ...'; A god (Enki) gives the king broad understanding and knowledge of everything; Who shall ascend the mountain of YHWH? He who has clean hands and a pure heart and has not sworn deceitfully; A god chooses the king 'in his heart' (šag4 pad3); The divine River of the Ordeal (Id-lurugu) clears the just man and catches the evil; A god formally decrees (nam tar) a good destiny for the king: heroism, long reign, splendour.

Only in Hear, O heavens; the great indictment, sacrifice rejected, the faithful city: City or people given a new name in the future age (e.g. 'City of Righteousness', 'Hephzibah'); The faithful city has become a harlot; silver turned to dross, wine diluted with water; Worshippers shamed by the sacred oaks (elim) and gardens they chose; Daughter Zion left alone like a booth in a vineyard, a hut in a cucumber field, a besieged city; Nation pictured as a body beaten from sole of foot to head, with untended wounds and sores; Sky and earth 'listen to their Lord' (adhinat) and are made to obey at the end; Israel likened to a donkey that knows, or does not understand, what it has [divergence between the texts]; Prophet addresses his own rulers and people as 'Sodom' and 'Gomorrah'; In Lot's town only one house of submitters (muslimin) was found, and the believers were brought out; Book or oracle opens with a heading naming the prophet, his father and the kings in whose days he saw the vision; God's people as sons he reared who rebelled against him; Though sins be like scarlet they shall be white as snow; though red as crimson, like wool; and 12 more.

sides.note: A building whose top reaches the midst of heaven. Enlil's E-kur is praised for it, its radiance touching heaven; Pharaoh's ṣarḥ, meant to reach heaven and look at the God of Moses, is his evil deed made fair to him.

passages.text: וַיֹּאמְר֞וּ הָ֣בָה נִבְנֶה לָּ֣נוּ עִ֗יר וּמִגְדָּל֙ וְרֹאשׁ֣וֹ בַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וְנַֽעֲשֶׂה לָּ֖נוּ שֵׁ֑ם פֶּן נָפ֖וּץ עַל פְּנֵ֥י כָל הָאָֽרֶץ
וַיֵּ֣רֶד יְהוָ֔ה לִרְאֹ֥ת אֶת הָעִ֖יר וְאֶת הַמִּגְדָּ֑ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנ֖וּ בְּנֵ֥י הָאָדָֽם
וַיָּ֨פֶץ יְהוָ֥ה אֹתָ֛ם מִשָּׁ֖ם עַל פְּנֵ֣י כָל הָאָ֑רֶץ וַֽיַּחְדְּל֖וּ לִבְנֹ֥ת הָעִֽיר

sides.note: A tower toward heaven: Babel's builders, all humankind (hāvâ nivneh llānû ʿîr û-migdāl wə-rōʾšô vaš-šāmayim), want to make a name and not be scattered; God comes down to see, and scatters them. In the Quran one king orders it of his minister (fa-jʿal lī ṣarḥan laʿallī aṭṭaliʿu ilā ilāhi Mūsā wa-innī la-aẓunnuhu mina l-kādhibīna): the aim is to climb up and look at Moses' God, mockingly. The ending is drowning (fa-nabadhnāhum fī l-yamm), not dispersal. God's descent to inspect the tower (wa-yyēred YHWH lirʾōt) is reversed into Pharaoh's wish to ascend and inspect God.

Only in A shir-namshub to Inana, segment A - Inana's self-praise (Inana I): The goddess calls herself 'the milk of the god' (of Dumuzid); A deity says the mountains are in her hand and at her feet, with a foreign land (Elam) in her grip; A goddess describes herself in an 'I am' litany of roles she plays in each place: in battle, in the alehouse, at the gate; The goddess promises to go before the king in battle, carry his weapon and be his advocate in the assembly; Boast: the other gods are small birds, I am the falcon; the gods butt one another, I am the wild cow; Heaven and earth placed on, or held in, the deity's head, hand or feet; Inana (evening star) is the prostitute who goes to the tavern and is food to the poor; Litany of 'I am': the king lists, god by god, how each high deity chose, endowed or cherished him.

Only in Ištar's sovereignty and her great names (Hymn to the Queen of Nippur): The great gods each give a deity a great name in turn, and the Igigi proclaim her seven names; The gods' powers and functions are taken up by and entrusted to one god, who is called simply 'the Lord'; A goddess has the power to turn man into woman and woman into man, put spindles in men's hands and weapons in women's hands; Offerings, incense and libations to the 'Queen of Heaven'; Inana is titled lady, queen or mother of heaven (nin/ama an-na, 'queen of heaven'); Hymnic refrain to the king: 'Who is as mighty as you, who rivals you?'.

Šamaš ... your name is indeed Marduk': Syncretistic litany: each great god (Anšar, Dagan, Adad, Nannar, Šamaš, Erra, Ningirsu) is declared to be a name or aspect of the one supreme god: 'your name is X ... your name is indeed Marduk'; The supreme god alone holds the rope (ṣerretu) or bond of heaven and earth, his sceptre laid across the netherworld; YHWH rides on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; Egypt's idols tremble before him; How thunder in the clouds relates to the god: his own roar or a creature praising him [shared matter] [divergence between the texts]; Whatever name is pronounced, it belongs to the one god: 'he is our god' / 'his are the beautiful names' [divergence between the texts]; The god is creator of everything, without whom nothing whatsoever was formed and no lord could exist; The god's command cannot be altered and his assent cannot be changed; The god (alone) holds the heavens (and earth) in place: the bond or rope of heaven, holding back the sky; At the storm god's roar from the clouds heaven and earth shake, mountains quake and the seas are stirred up; Each line of a litany is repeated for one god under several names (Ninurta, Pabilsaĝ, Ninĝirsu), identifying them; The sun god is the king of justice who illuminates the land like a torch and assures the king's just rule; The moon god renews his light, born every month, light of heaven and earth; and 2 more.

Enjoy the day: Human life passes like the twinkling of an eye; A day of happiness is worth more than tens of thousands of years of silence (death); life without cheer is no better than death; A primeval king is said to have reigned tens of thousands of years (e.g. 36,000); 'Where are' the famous kings of old (who reigned thousands of years, who ascended to heaven, who sought life)? They are gone and none can reach them; A span of many years is set against a single day [divergence between the texts]; Who has gone up to heaven and come down, gathered the wind in his fists, wrapped the waters in a garment? What is his name and his son's name?; The gods grant the flood hero life like a god, eternal life.

Only in Wise and fool share one fate; hatred of toil; eat and drink: The speaker says 'I hated life' because all is vapor; All his days are pain and vexation; even at night his heart does not rest; God gives the sinner the task of gathering and heaping up to give to the one who pleases God; Hating his toil because he must leave it to one who comes after him, who may be wise or a fool; Wisdom excels folly as light excels darkness; the wise has eyes in his head, the fool walks in darkness; Whether the seeing and the blind, light and darkness, end alike [divergence between the texts]; There is no remembrance of former people nor will there be of those yet to come; The good leaves an inheritance to his grandchildren; the sinner's wealth is stored up for the righteous; One fate (miqreh) befalls the wise and the fool, man and beast alike; Wise men die, the fool and the brute perish together and leave their wealth to others.

Only in Proverbs collection 14, sources B-C: Enlil's temple, the palace, wives and children, the malicious spouse, the stranger leader: Saying: both the palace and the netherworld (iri11-gal) require obedience from their inhabitants; Saying: the E-babbar that Mesilim built was destroyed by Nanni, a man whose seed was cut off; Children come from the divine, as a gift; Saying: a stranger (gir5) is the leader in a foreign city; Saying: Enlil's temple is a summation of accounts with the temple manager as overseer, a gathering of wages; One's wife or child can be one's worst affliction or enemy; Saying: a malicious wife living in the house is the worst of all afflictions; woe to one who married a malicious husband or bore a malicious son; Saying: a plant as sweet as a husband does not grow in the desert; my husband heaps up for me, my child measures out, my lover picks the bones from the fish; Fable: the pig squeals on its way to slaughter and the butcher tells it that its ancestors and forebears walked the same road; Saying: having wives is human, having children is from the gods; A quarrelsome wife is like a continual dripping (of a leaking roof); Sayings on the palace (e2-gal): it cannot ignore waste land; it is an ox to be caught by the tail; one day a mother giving birth, the next a mother in mourning; a slippery place; like the netherworld it demands obedience; and 3 more.

Only in Psalm 127, unless YHWH builds the house; sons as arrows: Sons of one's youth will not be put to shame when they speak with enemies in the gate; 'Unless YHWH builds the house, its builders labor in vain; unless YHWH guards the city, the watchman wakes in vain'; Rising early and toiling is vain; God gives (in) sleep to his beloved (yedido); Superscription 'A song of ascents' (shir ha-ma'alot), Ps 120-134.
